skeleton.name: Skeleton
skeleton.summary: Bones and cartilage: the body's load-bearing frame.
skeleton.overview: The adult skeleton has 206 bones plus the cartilages that cap joints, join the ribs to the sternum and shape the nose and airway. It is organised into an axial skeleton (skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum) that protects the brain, spinal cord, heart and lungs, and an appendicular skeleton (the limbs with their girdles) built for movement. Bone is living tissue: it remodels throughout life in response to load, stores calcium and phosphate, and houses the marrow that makes blood cells.
functions: Supports the body and gives it shape
Protects the brain, spinal cord and thoracic organs
Provides levers and attachment points for muscles
Stores calcium and phosphate
Houses red marrow, the site of blood cell production
clinical: Fractures follow trauma or weakened bone (osteoporosis)
Osteoarthritis wears the articular cartilage of weight-bearing joints
Scoliosis, kyphosis and disc disease affect the vertebral column

joints.name: Joints & ligaments
joints.summary: Ligaments, joint capsules, discs and membranes that bind the skeleton.
joints.overview: Where bones meet, connective tissue holds them together and limits their motion. Ligaments are dense bands of collagen running bone to bone; intervertebral discs are fibrocartilage cushions between vertebral bodies; interosseous membranes bind the paired bones of the forearm and leg. BodyParts3D models a selection of these structures, including every intervertebral disc, the plantar ligaments of the foot and the check ligaments of the eye muscles.
functions: Stabilise joints while allowing controlled movement
Absorb and distribute load between bones
Transmit forces along the limbs
clinical: Ligament sprains and tears (for example the knee's cruciate ligaments)
Herniated intervertebral discs can compress nerve roots
Degenerative disc disease narrows the space between vertebrae

teeth.name: Teeth
teeth.summary: The permanent dentition: 32 teeth of the upper and lower jaws.
teeth.overview: Adults have up to 32 permanent teeth: in each quadrant two incisors, one canine, two premolars and three molars. Incisors cut, canines tear, premolars and molars grind. Each tooth has a crown covered by enamel, the hardest tissue in the body, a root anchored in the jaw by the periodontal ligament, and a pulp cavity carrying vessels and nerves. This model includes 28 teeth; the third molars (wisdom teeth) are absent.
functions: Cut, tear and grind food to begin digestion
Support speech and the shape of the face
clinical: Dental caries dissolves enamel and dentine
Periodontal disease loosens the tooth's attachment
Impacted wisdom teeth are a common reason for extraction

muscles.name: Muscles
muscles.summary: Skeletal muscles, tendons and aponeuroses that move the body.
muscles.overview: Skeletal muscle makes up roughly 40% of body mass. Each muscle spans one or more joints, attaching to bone through tendons or flat aponeuroses; when its fibres shorten it pulls the bones together. Muscles work in groups: agonists produce a movement, antagonists control it, and stabilisers hold neighbouring joints still. The model includes the muscles of the limbs, trunk, neck, face, larynx and pharynx, and the diaphragm.
functions: Produce movement and maintain posture
Stabilise joints
Drive breathing (diaphragm and intercostals)
Generate heat
clinical: Strains and tears from overload
Compartment syndrome when pressure rises within a fascial compartment
Muscular dystrophies progressively weaken muscle fibres

heart.name: Heart
heart.summary: Chambers, valves and walls of the heart, with the pericardium.
heart.overview: The heart is a four-chambered muscular pump about the size of a fist. The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the venae cavae and passes it through the tricuspid valve to the right ventricle, which pumps it to the lungs. Oxygenated blood returns to the left atrium, crosses the mitral valve into the thick-walled left ventricle and is ejected through the aortic valve into the aorta. The model separates the atrial and ventricular walls, the chambers, the valve leaflets and cusps, and the papillary muscles that anchor the mitral and tricuspid valves.
functions: Pump blood through the pulmonary and systemic circulations
Keep blood flowing one way with four valves
Generate its own rhythm through the conduction system
clinical: Coronary artery disease and myocardial infarction
Heart failure when the ventricles cannot pump enough
Valve disease: stenosis or regurgitation
Arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation
keyStructures: Anterior papillary muscle of right ventricle

arteries.name: Arteries
arteries.summary: Systemic and pulmonary arteries carrying blood away from the heart.
arteries.overview: Arteries carry blood away from the heart under pressure. The aorta leaves the left ventricle, arches over the heart giving off the vessels to the head and arms, then descends through the thorax and abdomen before dividing into the iliac arteries for the pelvis and legs. The pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. With 642 modelled pieces, this is the largest layer in the atlas, down to the segmental arteries of the lungs, liver and kidneys and the small branches on the surface of the brain.
functions: Distribute oxygenated blood to every organ
Regulate blood pressure and flow through muscular walls
Carry deoxygenated blood to the lungs (pulmonary arteries)
clinical: Atherosclerosis narrows arteries and can cause heart attack or stroke
Aneurysms are dangerous dilatations, most often of the abdominal aorta
Peripheral arterial disease limits blood flow to the legs

veins.name: Veins
veins.summary: Systemic and pulmonary veins returning blood to the heart.
veins.overview: Veins return blood to the heart at low pressure, helped by valves and by the squeeze of surrounding muscles. Deep veins run alongside the arteries; superficial veins such as the cephalic, basilic and saphenous veins lie just under the skin. Blood from the gut drains first to the liver through the hepatic portal vein before joining the inferior vena cava. The pulmonary veins are the exception to the rule: they carry oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.
functions: Return blood to the heart
Act as a reservoir holding most of the blood volume
Route nutrient-rich blood from the gut through the liver (portal system)
clinical: Deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism
Varicose veins from failing valves in the superficial veins
Portal hypertension in liver disease

nervous.name: Nervous system
nervous.summary: Brain, spinal cord, cranial and spinal nerves, ganglia and meninges.
nervous.overview: The nervous system gathers information, decides and commands. The brain and spinal cord form the central nervous system; the cranial and spinal nerves with their ganglia form the peripheral nervous system. This model is richest in the head: the cerebral gyri and lobes, the basal ganglia, thalamus and hypothalamus, the brainstem and cerebellum, the ventricles, the optic pathway and the nerves of the orbit. Peripheral nerves of the limbs are not part of this BodyParts3D release.
functions: Sense the environment and the body's internal state
Integrate information, memory and emotion
Control voluntary and involuntary movement
Regulate organs through the autonomic system
clinical: Stroke: loss of blood supply to part of the brain
Epilepsy, migraine and neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson's
Nerve compression syndromes and neuropathies

sensory.name: Sensory organs
sensory.summary: Eyes and ears with their internal structures.
sensory.overview: The eye focuses light through the cornea and lens onto the retina, whose signals travel along the optic nerve to the brain. The model separates the cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, lens, vitreous body and retina, plus the lacrimal apparatus that produces and drains tears and the tarsal plates of the eyelids. The external ear collects sound towards the tympanic membrane; the middle and inner ear are not modelled in this release.
functions: Vision: focusing and detecting light
Protecting and lubricating the eye (eyelids, tears)
Hearing and balance (ear)
clinical: Refractive errors, cataract and glaucoma
Retinal detachment and macular degeneration
Conjunctivitis and blocked tear ducts

respiratory.name: Respiratory
respiratory.summary: Nose, larynx, trachea, bronchial tree and lungs.
respiratory.overview: Air enters through the nose, where cartilages support the nostrils and conchae warm and moisten it, passes the larynx, which guards the airway and produces the voice, and descends the trachea. The trachea divides into the main bronchi, which branch again and again into the segmental bronchial trees modelled here, one for each bronchopulmonary segment. Gas exchange takes place in the alveoli at the end of this tree; the lung tissue itself is not a separate piece in this dataset, so the bronchial trees stand in for the lungs.
functions: Bring oxygen into the blood and remove carbon dioxide
Filter, warm and humidify inhaled air
Produce the voice (larynx)
Help regulate blood acidity
clinical: Asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease narrow the airways
Pneumonia infects the alveoli
Lung cancer most often arises in the bronchi

digestive.name: Digestive
digestive.summary: Mouth, pharynx, oesophagus, stomach, intestines, liver, pancreas.
digestive.overview: The digestive tract is a nine-metre tube from mouth to anus. Food is chewed, swallowed down the oesophagus, churned with acid in the stomach, digested and absorbed along the small intestine (duodenum, jejunum, ileum), and its residue concentrated in the colon. The liver, gallbladder and pancreas pour bile and enzymes into the duodenum. The model includes the tongue, salivary glands and gums, the stomach and intestines in many segments, the liver as eight hepatovenous segments with its bile ducts, the gallbladder, the pancreas and the mesenteries that suspend the gut.
functions: Break food down mechanically and chemically
Absorb nutrients and water
Store and release energy (liver)
Eliminate waste
clinical: Reflux, gastritis and peptic ulcers
Appendicitis, inflammatory bowel disease and colorectal cancer
Gallstones, hepatitis and pancreatitis

urinary.name: Urinary
urinary.overview: The two kidneys filter about 180 litres of plasma a day, returning almost all of it to the blood and excreting the rest as urine. Urine drains through the ureters into the bladder, a muscular reservoir that empties through the urethra. The kidneys also regulate blood pressure, red cell production and vitamin D activation.
functions: Filter waste from the blood
Balance water, salts and acidity
Regulate blood pressure
Store and expel urine
clinical: Urinary tract infections
Kidney stones
Chronic kidney disease and dialysis

reproductive.name: Reproductive
reproductive.summary: The organs of sex, fertility and reproduction: ovaries, uterus, vagina, vulva and breasts; testes, prostate and penis; and the anatomy of gender-affirming care.
reproductive.overview: The reproductive system makes gametes and sex hormones and carries, delivers and feeds a pregnancy. On the female side the ovaries release an egg each cycle and make oestrogen and progesterone; the fallopian tubes carry the egg to the uterus, whose lining is shed each month as a period or supports a pregnancy; the cervix, vagina and vulva form the birth canal and external genitalia; and the breasts make milk. On the male side the testes produce sperm and testosterone, the epididymis and deferent ducts store and carry sperm, the seminal vesicles and prostate add most of the seminal fluid, and the erectile bodies of the penis deliver it. BodyParts3D, the dataset behind the 3D atlas, was built from one adult male, so only the male organs are modelled in 3D; the female organs, the breasts and the surgically constructed anatomy of gender-affirming surgery (neovagina, neophallus) have full written anatomy pages that show the modelled pelvis and chest around them.
functions: Produce eggs or sperm and the sex hormones oestrogen, progesterone and testosterone
Carry, nourish and deliver a pregnancy, and make milk
Deliver sperm and seminal fluid
Drive puberty and the secondary sexual characteristics
clinical: Endometriosis, fibroids and polycystic ovary syndrome
Breast, cervical and ovarian cancer, and the screening programmes that find them early
Ectopic pregnancy is an emergency
Benign prostatic enlargement and prostate cancer
Testicular torsion is a surgical emergency
Gender-affirming hormones and surgery change which organs are present: screening and care follow the anatomy a person has

endocrine.name: Endocrine
endocrine.summary: Hormone-producing glands: thyroid, adrenal, pituitary, pineal.
endocrine.overview: Endocrine glands release hormones into the blood to regulate metabolism, growth, stress responses and reproduction. The pituitary, hanging from the base of the brain, controls most other glands. The adrenal glands cap the kidneys, producing cortisol, aldosterone and adrenaline. The pineal body, which sets the sleep-wake rhythm, is modelled with the brain; the thyroid gland is not included in this release.
functions: Coordinate metabolism, growth and stress responses
Regulate salt, water and blood pressure (adrenal cortex)
Control other glands (pituitary)
clinical: Diabetes mellitus
Thyroid over- and under-activity
Adrenal insufficiency and Cushing's syndrome

lymphatic.name: Lymphatic & immune
lymphatic.overview: Lymphatic vessels return tissue fluid to the blood and carry it through lymph nodes where immune cells inspect it. The spleen filters blood, recycles old red cells and mounts immune responses; the thymus, large in childhood, trains T lymphocytes. This release models the spleen and the two lobes of the thymus; lymph nodes and lymphatic vessels are not included.
functions: Return tissue fluid to the circulation
Filter blood and lymph
Produce and mature immune cells
clinical: Lymphoma and leukaemia
Splenic rupture after abdominal trauma
Lymphoedema when drainage is blocked

skin.name: Skin
skin.overview: The skin is the body's largest organ, about two square metres of barrier against infection, injury and water loss. Its outer epidermis constantly renews; the dermis beneath carries vessels, nerves, glands and hair follicles. In the atlas the skin is a single surface shown as a translucent overlay so the structures beneath stay visible; hair of the head, eyebrows and pubic hair are separate pieces.
functions: Protect against infection, injury and dehydration
Sense touch, pressure, temperature and pain
Regulate body temperature through sweat and blood flow
Make vitamin D
clinical: Eczema, psoriasis and acne
Skin cancers, including melanoma
Burns and wound healing

organs.name: Brain
organs.summary: The cerebrum, cerebellum and brainstem: about 1.4 kg of tissue that controls thought, movement, sensation and every organ.

article.title: Brain Anatomy
article.descriptor: Lobes, Deep Structures, Blood Supply & Function
article.intro: The brain is about 1.4 kg of nervous tissue floating in cerebrospinal fluid inside the skull. Its wrinkled cerebral hemispheres handle perception, movement, language, memory and planning; the cerebellum coordinates movement; and the brainstem keeps breathing, heart rate and consciousness going.

keyFacts.label: Weight
keyFacts.value: About 1.3-1.4 kg, 2% of body weight, using 20% of the body's oxygen

keyFacts.label: Main parts
keyFacts.value: Cerebrum (two hemispheres), diencephalon (thalamus, hypothalamus), brainstem (midbrain, pons, medulla), cerebellum

keyFacts.label: Lobes
keyFacts.value: Frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital, plus the insula and limbic lobe

keyFacts.label: Blood supply
keyFacts.value: Two internal carotid and two vertebral arteries joining at the circle of Willis

keyFacts.label: Protection
keyFacts.value: Skull, three meninges and about 150 mL of cerebrospinal fluid

keyFacts.label: Neurons
keyFacts.value: Roughly 86 billion

sections.heading: Location and coverings
sections.body: The brain fills the cranial cavity and is wrapped in three meninges: the tough dura mater lining the skull, the spidery arachnoid, and the delicate pia mater clinging to every fold. Cerebrospinal fluid made in the ventricles circulates in the subarachnoid space between arachnoid and pia, cushioning the brain and reducing its effective weight to a few tens of grams. The brain leaves the skull through the foramen magnum as the spinal cord.

sections.heading: Cerebral hemispheres and lobes
sections.body: Each hemisphere is folded into gyri separated by sulci, which triples the surface area of the cortex. The central sulcus divides the frontal lobe (movement, planning, speech production in Broca's area, personality) from the parietal lobe (touch, spatial awareness); the lateral sulcus marks off the temporal lobe (hearing, language comprehension in Wernicke's area, memory via the hippocampus); the occipital lobe at the back is vision. The precentral gyrus is the primary motor cortex and the postcentral gyrus the primary somatosensory cortex, each mapping the opposite side of the body. The corpus callosum, a thick band of white matter, connects the two hemispheres.

sections.heading: Deep structures
sections.body: Beneath the cortex lie the basal ganglia (caudate nucleus, putamen, globus pallidus), which shape movement and are lost in Parkinson's disease; the thalamus, the relay station for almost all sensation on its way to the cortex; and the hypothalamus, which controls hunger, thirst, temperature, sleep and the pituitary gland below it. The hippocampus and amygdala in the medial temporal lobe form new memories and process emotion.

sections.heading: Brainstem and cerebellum
sections.body: The midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata carry every tract between the brain and spinal cord and house the nuclei of ten of the twelve cranial nerves, the breathing and cardiovascular centres, and the reticular formation that maintains wakefulness. The cerebellum, tucked beneath the occipital lobes, compares intended with actual movement and corrects it, giving smooth, coordinated action and balance.

sections.heading: Blood supply
sections.body: The internal carotid arteries supply the front two-thirds of each hemisphere through the anterior and middle cerebral arteries; the vertebral arteries join to form the basilar artery, which supplies the brainstem, cerebellum and, through the posterior cerebral arteries, the occipital lobes. These vessels meet at the circle of Willis on the underside of the brain, a ring that can partly compensate for a blocked artery. The middle cerebral artery is the vessel most often blocked in stroke; because it supplies the motor and language areas, its blockage causes the face, arm and speech signs of the FAST test.

sections.heading: Venous drainage
sections.body: Cerebral veins drain into the dural venous sinuses, channels between the layers of dura: the superior sagittal sinus along the top of the brain, the transverse and sigmoid sinuses curving down to become the internal jugular veins. Cerebrospinal fluid is absorbed into the same sinuses through arachnoid granulations.

sections.heading: Function
sections.body: Sensory information from the body crosses to the opposite hemisphere, so the left brain controls and feels the right side of the body. Language is usually left-hemisphere dominant. Neurons communicate with electrical impulses and chemical neurotransmitters; the pattern of connections, refined throughout life, underlies learning and memory.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Stroke, tumours, trauma, infection and degenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's each damage particular regions, and the resulting deficits map back onto the anatomy: weakness from the motor cortex or internal capsule, memory loss from the hippocampus, tremor and rigidity from the basal ganglia, unsteadiness from the cerebellum. Raised pressure inside the rigid skull, from bleeding or swelling, is dangerous because the brain can be pushed through the openings in the dura and the foramen magnum.

organs.name: Cerebellum
organs.summary: The 'little brain' behind the brainstem coordinates balance, posture and the timing of movements.

organs.name: Brainstem
organs.summary: Midbrain, pons and medulla connect the brain to the spinal cord and run breathing, heart rate and consciousness.

organs.name: Eye
organs.summary: The eyeball and its parts: cornea, lens, iris, retina and the tissues that protect and move it.

organs.name: Ear
organs.summary: The external ear gathers sound; the middle and inner ear (not modelled here) convert it to nerve signals and sense balance.

organs.name: Nose
organs.summary: Nasal bones and cartilages shape the nose; the conchae inside warm and filter the air.

organs.name: Tongue
organs.summary: A muscular organ for taste, chewing, swallowing and speech.

organs.name: Larynx
organs.summary: The voice box: a cartilage frame with the vocal ligaments, guarding the airway and producing sound.

organs.name: Trachea & bronchial tree
organs.summary: The windpipe and the branching airways that carry air into every segment of the lungs.

organs.name: Lungs
organs.summary: Two spongy organs of gas exchange. This dataset models the lungs through their segmental bronchial trees and pulmonary vessels rather than as solid lobes.

article.title: Lung Anatomy
article.descriptor: Lobes, Airways, Blood Supply & Gas Exchange
article.intro: The lungs are two spongy, cone-shaped organs filling most of the chest on either side of the heart. Air reaches them through a branching tree of airways ending in about 300 million alveoli, whose combined surface, roughly the size of a tennis court, is where oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves it.

keyFacts.label: Lobes
keyFacts.value: Three on the right (upper, middle, lower), two on the left (upper, lower) with a lingula

keyFacts.label: Airways
keyFacts.value: Trachea, main bronchi, lobar and segmental bronchi, bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveoli

keyFacts.label: Segments
keyFacts.value: 10 bronchopulmonary segments per lung, each with its own bronchus and artery

keyFacts.label: Blood supply
keyFacts.value: Pulmonary arteries (for gas exchange) and bronchial arteries (for the lung tissue itself)

keyFacts.label: Nerve supply
keyFacts.value: Vagus nerve (constricts airways, mucus) and sympathetic fibres (dilate airways)

keyFacts.label: Breathing
keyFacts.value: About 12-16 breaths a minute at rest, 500 mL each

sections.heading: Location and pleura
sections.body: Each lung sits in its own pleural cavity, wrapped in visceral pleura that is continuous with the parietal pleura lining the chest wall, diaphragm and mediastinum. The thin film of fluid between the two layers lets the lung slide as the chest expands and holds it against the chest wall by surface tension, so that when the diaphragm descends the lung is pulled open. Air entering this space (a pneumothorax) breaks the seal and the lung collapses. The right lung is larger and shorter, pushed up by the liver; the left has a cardiac notch that makes room for the heart.

sections.heading: Lobes and segments
sections.body: Fissures divide the right lung into upper, middle and lower lobes and the left into upper and lower lobes. Each lobe is built from bronchopulmonary segments, pyramids of lung tissue with their own segmental bronchus and artery and no connection to their neighbours, which is why surgeons can remove one segment and radiologists describe a shadow by segment.

sections.heading: Airways
sections.body: The trachea divides at the carina into right and left main bronchi. The right is wider and more vertical, so inhaled objects usually go that way. Each main bronchus divides into lobar, then segmental bronchi, then some twenty further generations of ever-smaller bronchi and bronchioles. Cartilage rings stiffen the larger airways; smooth muscle in the bronchioles adjusts their calibre, tightening in asthma. Ciliated cells and mucus sweep dust and microbes upward to be swallowed. Beyond the terminal bronchioles, respiratory bronchioles and alveolar ducts open into clusters of alveoli.

sections.heading: Alveoli and gas exchange
sections.body: An alveolus is a thin-walled sac about 0.2 mm across, lined by flat type I cells for gas exchange and type II cells that secrete surfactant, the detergent that stops the sacs collapsing at the end of each breath. Capillaries form a dense net around every alveolus, so the barrier between air and blood is under a micrometre thick. Oxygen diffuses into red cells and binds haemoglobin; carbon dioxide diffuses the other way and is breathed out.

sections.heading: Blood supply
sections.body: The pulmonary trunk from the right ventricle divides into right and left pulmonary arteries, which follow the bronchi into every segment and carry deoxygenated blood to the alveolar capillaries. Four pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood to the left atrium. Separately, small bronchial arteries from the aorta nourish the bronchi and lung tissue. A clot lodging in a pulmonary artery (pulmonary embolism) blocks flow to the segment it serves.

sections.heading: Innervation
sections.body: The pulmonary plexus around each lung root carries parasympathetic fibres from the vagus nerve, which constrict the airways and stimulate mucus, and sympathetic fibres, which relax airway muscle. Salbutamol and adrenaline relieve wheeze by acting on the same beta-2 receptors that the sympathetic nerves use. The lung itself has no pain fibres; chest pain from lung disease comes from the parietal pleura, supplied by the intercostal and phrenic nerves.

sections.heading: Function
sections.body: Breathing in is active: the diaphragm flattens and the external intercostals lift the ribs, enlarging the chest so air flows in. Breathing out at rest is passive elastic recoil. The brainstem sets the rhythm, driven mainly by the level of carbon dioxide in the blood. Beyond gas exchange the lungs filter small clots, make angiotensin-converting enzyme, and defend against inhaled microbes.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Asthma and COPD narrow the airways; pneumonia fills alveoli with fluid and pus; fibrosis stiffens the lung; emphysema destroys alveolar walls; cancer most often arises from the bronchial lining. Spirometry measures how much and how fast air moves; a chest X-ray and CT show the lobes, segments and pleural spaces; a pulse oximeter reads how well the alveoli are loading oxygen onto haemoglobin.

references.title: NIH NHLBI: How the lungs work
Asthma + Lung UK: How your lungs work

organs.name: Heart
organs.summary: The four-chambered pump that drives blood around the body.

article.title: Heart Anatomy
article.intro: The heart is a fist-sized muscular pump in the middle of the chest, tilted so that two-thirds of it lies to the left of the midline. Its four chambers and four valves move about five litres of blood every minute at rest, sending deoxygenated blood to the lungs and oxygenated blood to the rest of the body.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: Middle mediastinum, behind the sternum, between the lungs, resting on the diaphragm

keyFacts.label: Chambers
keyFacts.value: Right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, left ventricle

keyFacts.label: Valves
keyFacts.value: Tricuspid, pulmonary, mitral, aortic

keyFacts.label: Weight
keyFacts.value: About 250-350 g in adults

keyFacts.label: Blood supply
keyFacts.value: Right and left coronary arteries from the ascending aorta

keyFacts.label: Nerve supply
keyFacts.value: Sympathetic fibres (speed up) and the vagus nerve (slow down) via the cardiac plexus

keyFacts.label: Output
keyFacts.value: About 5 L/min at rest, up to 25 L/min in exercise

sections.heading: Location and coverings
sections.body: The heart sits in the middle mediastinum, enclosed in the pericardium: a tough fibrous outer sac fused to the diaphragm below and the great vessels above, lined by a double layer of serous membrane whose thin film of fluid lets the heart beat almost without friction. The apex points down and to the left, reaching the fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line, where the apex beat can be felt. The base faces backwards, towards the oesophagus and descending aorta, which is why an oesophageal ultrasound probe gives such clear views of the atria.

sections.heading: Chambers
sections.body: The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the superior and inferior venae cavae and the coronary sinus, and passes it through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, a thin-walled crescent-shaped chamber that pumps into the pulmonary trunk. The left atrium receives oxygenated blood through four pulmonary veins and fills the left ventricle, whose wall is about three times thicker than the right because it must generate pressures of 120 mmHg or more to drive blood around the whole body. The interatrial and interventricular septa separate the two sides; the foramen ovale, open before birth, leaves a small depression in the interatrial septum.

sections.heading: Valves
sections.body: Two atrioventricular valves (the tricuspid on the right and the mitral, with two leaflets, on the left) are held closed during ventricular contraction by chordae tendineae anchored to papillary muscles, so they cannot balloon back into the atria. Two semilunar valves (pulmonary and aortic), each with three cusps, prevent blood ejected from the ventricles from flowing back. The valve rings sit in a fibrous skeleton that also insulates the atria electrically from the ventricles, so that the only electrical route between them is the atrioventricular node and bundle.

sections.heading: Blood supply
sections.body: The right and left coronary arteries arise from the aortic sinuses just above the aortic valve and fill mainly during diastole. The left coronary artery divides within a few centimetres into the anterior interventricular (left anterior descending) artery, running down the front of the interventricular septum, and the circumflex artery, curving round in the left atrioventricular groove. The right coronary artery runs in the right atrioventricular groove, usually giving off the sinoatrial nodal artery and, in most people, the posterior interventricular artery that supplies the inferior wall. Blockage of any of these branches starves a predictable territory of muscle.

sections.heading: Venous drainage
sections.body: Most venous blood from the heart wall collects in the coronary sinus, a wide vein in the posterior atrioventricular groove that empties into the right atrium; the great, middle and small cardiac veins are its main tributaries. Small anterior cardiac veins and the tiny thebesian veins drain directly into the chambers.

sections.heading: Innervation and conduction
sections.body: The heart beats on its own: the sinoatrial node in the right atrial wall near the superior vena cava fires about 70 times a minute, the impulse spreads across the atria to the atrioventricular node, pauses, then races down the bundle of His and its branches to the ventricular muscle. The autonomic nervous system only modulates this rhythm. Sympathetic fibres from the upper thoracic spinal cord increase rate and force; parasympathetic fibres in the vagus nerve slow it. Pain from the heart is referred to the chest, left arm, neck and jaw because those areas share spinal cord segments with the cardiac sympathetic nerves.

sections.heading: Function
sections.body: Each cardiac cycle has a filling phase (diastole) and a contraction phase (systole). The right side of the heart sends blood through the pulmonary circulation to pick up oxygen and unload carbon dioxide; the left side sends it through the systemic circulation. Cardiac output is heart rate multiplied by stroke volume, and both are adjusted continuously by nerves, hormones and the volume of blood returning to the heart.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Narrowing of the coronary arteries causes angina and heart attacks; the territory affected shows on the ECG and echocardiogram. Valve disease (a leaking mitral valve, a narrowed aortic valve) can be heard as murmurs and measured with ultrasound. Failure of the pump causes fluid to back up into the lungs and legs. Disorders of the conduction system cause slow, fast or irregular rhythms such as atrial fibrillation. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation works because the heart lies directly behind the lower sternum, where compressions squeeze it against the spine.

references.title: British Heart Foundation: How a healthy heart works
NIH NHLBI: How the heart works

organs.name: Coronary vessels
organs.summary: The arteries and veins that supply and drain the heart muscle itself.

article.title: Coronary Arteries Anatomy
article.intro: The coronary arteries are the heart's own blood supply: two vessels a few millimetres wide that arise from the aorta just above the aortic valve and run over the surface of the heart, sending branches into the muscle. Because each branch supplies a fixed territory, a blockage produces a predictable pattern of damage that the ECG, echocardiogram and angiogram can map.

keyFacts.label: Origin
keyFacts.value: Right and left aortic sinuses, just above the aortic valve

keyFacts.label: Left coronary artery
keyFacts.value: Short main stem dividing into the left anterior descending (anterior interventricular) and circumflex arteries

keyFacts.label: Right coronary artery
keyFacts.value: Runs in the right atrioventricular groove; gives the posterior interventricular artery in about 85% of people (right dominance)

keyFacts.label: Filling
keyFacts.value: Mainly during diastole, when the relaxed muscle lets blood through

keyFacts.label: Venous return
keyFacts.value: Great, middle and small cardiac veins to the coronary sinus

keyFacts.label: Flow
keyFacts.value: About 250 mL/min at rest, five times more in exercise

sections.heading: Left coronary artery
sections.body: The left main stem is only 1-2 cm long before it divides. The anterior interventricular branch, known clinically as the left anterior descending (LAD) artery, runs down the front of the interventricular groove to the apex, giving diagonal branches to the front of the left ventricle and septal branches into the septum; it supplies about half the left ventricle and most of the conduction bundles, which is why an LAD occlusion is the most dangerous heart attack. The circumflex artery curves round the left side in the atrioventricular groove, giving obtuse marginal branches to the lateral wall.

sections.heading: Right coronary artery
sections.body: The right coronary artery runs in the right atrioventricular groove, giving a branch to the sinoatrial node in most people, acute marginal branches to the right ventricle, and, in about 85% of people, the posterior interventricular (posterior descending) artery and a branch to the atrioventricular node. It supplies the right ventricle, the inferior wall of the left ventricle and the conduction nodes, so its blockage causes inferior infarcts often complicated by slow rhythms.

sections.heading: Dominance and variation
sections.body: The artery that gives off the posterior interventricular branch is called dominant: right in most people, left in about 8%, and shared in the rest. Anatomy varies enough that every angiogram is read individually. Collateral vessels between territories enlarge slowly when an artery narrows, which is why a chronic blockage can be survived while a sudden one is not.

sections.heading: Venous drainage
sections.body: The great cardiac vein accompanies the anterior interventricular artery and curves round with the circumflex into the coronary sinus, which runs in the posterior atrioventricular groove and empties into the right atrium; the middle cardiac vein follows the posterior interventricular artery. Pacing leads for heart failure are threaded through the coronary sinus to reach the left ventricle.

sections.heading: Physiology
sections.body: The coronary arteries are compressed by the contracting muscle, so most flow occurs in diastole. A fast heart rate shortens diastole and reduces supply just when demand rises. The vessels dilate in response to adenosine and nitric oxide released by working muscle; nitrates such as glyceryl trinitrate use the same pathway.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Fatty plaques in the wall narrow the lumen and cause angina on exertion; a ruptured plaque triggers a clot that blocks the artery and kills the muscle downstream within hours, a myocardial infarction. Troponin in the blood confirms damage, the ECG localises it, and an angiogram through a wrist or groin artery shows the blockage so that it can be opened with a balloon and stent or bypassed with a graft. Statins, aspirin and blood-pressure control slow the disease.

references.title: British Heart Foundation: Coronary heart disease

organs.name: Aorta
organs.summary: The largest artery, carrying blood from the left ventricle to the whole body.

article.title: Aorta Anatomy
article.intro: The aorta is the largest artery in the body, a thick elastic tube about 2.5-3 cm wide that carries every drop of oxygenated blood from the left ventricle. It rises from the heart, arches over it, and descends through the chest and abdomen, giving branches to every organ before dividing into the two common iliac arteries.

keyFacts.label: Segments
keyFacts.value: Ascending aorta, arch, descending thoracic aorta, abdominal aorta

keyFacts.label: Length
keyFacts.value: About 30-40 cm; ends at L4 by dividing into the common iliac arteries

keyFacts.label: Arch branches
keyFacts.value: Brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, left subclavian

keyFacts.label: Abdominal branches
keyFacts.value: Coeliac trunk, superior mesenteric, renal, gonadal and inferior mesenteric arteries

keyFacts.label: Wall
keyFacts.value: Three layers rich in elastin that store energy in systole and keep blood flowing in diastole

keyFacts.label: Pressure
keyFacts.value: About 120/80 mmHg at rest

sections.heading: Ascending aorta
sections.body: The aorta begins at the aortic valve inside the pericardium. Its first centimetres bulge into three aortic sinuses, from two of which the right and left coronary arteries arise, so the heart muscle is the first tissue the aorta supplies. The ascending aorta runs up and to the right for about 5 cm before curving into the arch.

sections.heading: Arch
sections.body: The arch passes backwards and to the left over the left main bronchus and the pulmonary trunk, at the level of the sternal angle, giving off three great branches from its upper surface: the brachiocephalic trunk (which divides into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries), the left common carotid artery and the left subclavian artery. Baroreceptors in the arch report blood pressure to the brainstem; the left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under it, so an enlarged arch can cause hoarseness.

sections.heading: Descending thoracic aorta
sections.body: From the arch the aorta descends on the left side of the spine, then behind the oesophagus, to pass through the diaphragm at T12. It gives posterior intercostal arteries to the chest wall, bronchial arteries to the lungs, oesophageal branches and small vessels to the pericardium and diaphragm.

sections.heading: Abdominal aorta
sections.body: In the abdomen the aorta lies to the left of the inferior vena cava, in front of the lumbar spine. Three unpaired branches supply the gut: the coeliac trunk (stomach, liver, spleen, pancreas), the superior mesenteric artery (small intestine and right colon) and the inferior mesenteric artery (left colon and rectum). Paired branches go to the adrenals, kidneys and gonads, and lumbar arteries to the back wall. At L4, level with the top of the hip bones, it divides into the common iliac arteries, which supply the pelvis and legs.

sections.heading: Wall structure and function
sections.body: The aortic wall has an inner intima, a thick media of elastic lamellae and smooth muscle, and an outer adventitia carrying its own tiny vessels. During systole the elastic wall stretches to accept the ejected blood; during diastole it recoils and keeps blood flowing forward, smoothing the pulse. With age the elastin fragments, the aorta stiffens and systolic pressure rises.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Atherosclerosis roughens the aorta and its branches; cholesterol and blood pressure drive it. An aneurysm, most often of the abdominal aorta below the kidneys, can rupture with catastrophic bleeding, which is why men over 65 are offered a screening ultrasound. Aortic dissection, a tear in the intima that lets blood split the wall, causes tearing chest pain radiating to the back and is a surgical emergency. Coarctation is a congenital narrowing near the arch. Aortic valve stenosis obstructs the outlet from the heart.

organs.name: Diaphragm
organs.summary: The dome-shaped muscle separating chest from abdomen; the main muscle of breathing.

organs.name: Pelvic floor
organs.summary: The levator ani (pubococcygeus, puborectalis, iliococcygeus) and coccygeus: a muscular hammock closing the bottom of the pelvis that supports the bladder, uterus or prostate and rectum and controls continence.

article.title: Pelvic Floor Anatomy
article.intro: The pelvic floor is a funnel-shaped sheet of skeletal muscle, mainly the levator ani and coccygeus on each side, that closes the lower opening of the bony pelvis and holds up the bladder, the rectum and, in women, the uterus and vagina. Everyone has one: it contracts to keep urine and faeces in and relaxes to let them out, stretches enormously in childbirth, and is weakened by pregnancy, ageing, straining and some operations.

keyFacts.label: Muscles
keyFacts.value: Levator ani (pubococcygeus with the puborectalis sling, and iliococcygeus) plus coccygeus on each side, together forming the pelvic diaphragm

keyFacts.label: Openings
keyFacts.value: The urogenital hiatus in front transmits the urethra and, in women, the vagina; the anal canal passes through the puborectalis sling behind

keyFacts.label: Below the diaphragm
keyFacts.value: The perineal membrane, the perineal body, the external urethral sphincter and the external anal sphincter

keyFacts.label: Nerve supply
keyFacts.value: Nerve to levator ani (S3-S4) on the upper surface and the pudendal nerve (S2-S4) on the lower surface and sphincters

keyFacts.label: Blood supply
keyFacts.value: Branches of the internal pudendal and inferior gluteal arteries, both from the internal iliac artery

keyFacts.label: Functions
keyFacts.value: Supports the pelvic organs against abdominal pressure, keeps urine and faeces in, stretches in childbirth, and helps sexual function and core stability

keyFacts.label: Training
keyFacts.value: Supervised pelvic floor muscle training for at least three months is first-line treatment for stress urinary incontinence

sections.heading: Location and relations
sections.body: The pelvic floor spans the pelvic outlet, the diamond-shaped opening bounded by the pubic symphysis in front, the ischial tuberosities at the sides and the coccyx behind. It is a bowl of muscle that slopes down and forwards from the pelvic walls to the midline, so the pelvic cavity above it holds the bladder, rectum and internal genital organs while the perineum lies below. On each side the sheet arises from the back of the pubic bone, from the tendinous arch of levator ani that runs across obturator internus, and from the ischial spine, and it inserts on the coccyx and the anococcygeal ligament. The bladder base rests on its anterior part, the prostate in men or the vagina and uterus in women lie in the middle, and the rectum bends forwards over the puborectalis sling. Below it lies the fat-filled ischioanal fossa, along whose lateral wall the pudendal nerve and vessels run.

sections.heading: Structure: levator ani, coccygeus and the perineum
sections.body: The pelvic diaphragm is formed by levator ani and, behind it, coccygeus. Pubococcygeus arises from the pubic bone and sweeps back to the coccyx; its most medial fibres, puborectalis, loop around the back of the anorectal junction as a U-shaped sling, and the fibres beside the urethra, vagina or prostate are named pubovaginalis or levator prostatae. Iliococcygeus arises further back from the tendinous arch and the ischial spine and forms the thinner lateral part. Coccygeus runs from the ischial spine to the lower sacrum and coccyx. The gap between the medial edges of the two levator ani muscles, the urogenital hiatus, transmits the urethra and, in women, the vagina, with the anal canal passing behind it. Beneath the front of the diaphragm the perineal membrane carries the external urethral sphincter, and the perineal body, between the anal canal and the vagina or bulb of the penis, anchors the perineal muscles and the external anal sphincter.

sections.heading: Blood supply and lymph
sections.body: The pelvic floor receives its blood from branches of the internal iliac artery. The internal pudendal artery leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen, passes round the ischial spine and re-enters through the lesser sciatic foramen to run in the pudendal canal along the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa; its inferior rectal branches supply the anal sphincter and the lower surface of levator ani, and its perineal branches the perineal muscles and the external genitalia. The inferior gluteal artery contributes to the upper, pelvic surface. Veins accompany the arteries to the internal iliac veins, and the venous plexuses around the rectum, prostate and vagina lie directly on the muscle sheet. Lymph from the deep pelvic structures drains to the internal iliac nodes, while lymph from the perineal skin and the lower anal canal drains to the superficial inguinal nodes, which is why a perineal infection can produce tender groin glands.

sections.heading: Innervation
sections.body: Levator ani is supplied on its pelvic surface by the nerve to levator ani, a direct branch of the sacral plexus from S3 and S4, and coccygeus by branches of S4 and S5. The perineal surface of puborectalis and the external anal sphincter receive fibres from the inferior rectal branch of the pudendal nerve (S2 to S4), which also supplies the external urethral sphincter and the perineal muscles and carries sensation from the perineum and the lower anal canal. Stretching of the pudendal nerve during a long or instrumental vaginal birth can leave it working poorly for months and contributes to incontinence. Damage to the sacral cord or the cauda equina removes both voluntary and reflex control and causes retention or incontinence. New difficulty passing urine or new incontinence with numbness around the genitals and inner thighs or new weakness in the legs can mean compression of the nerves at the base of the spine and needs emergency assessment straight away, at A&E or by calling 999.

sections.heading: Function
sections.body: Its resting tone holds the pelvic organs up against gravity and against the rises in intra-abdominal pressure produced by coughing, sneezing, lifting and straining, and it tightens reflexly just before such efforts. The puborectalis sling pulls the anorectal junction forwards, creating an angle that helps keep faeces in the rectum; the sling relaxes and the angle opens during defecation. Contraction of the anterior fibres compresses the urethra and supports the bladder neck, so that a cough does not force urine out. The muscles contract rhythmically during orgasm, and their tone contributes to sexual sensation. In labour the levator hiatus must stretch to several times its resting size to let the head of the baby pass, and the muscles usually recover over the following weeks to months, though the stretch can leave lasting weakness. It also forms the base of the abdominal cylinder with the diaphragm and abdominal wall.

sections.heading: Changes across life
sections.body: Pregnancy loads the floor and vaginal birth stretches it further: levator ani can tear from the pubic bone (levator avulsion), the anal sphincter can be torn and the pudendal nerve stretched, so leakage of urine after birth is common and usually improves with training. Chronic straining, a persistent cough, heavy lifting and obesity weaken it over years, and menopause thins the supporting tissues. Prostate removal takes away part of the urethral closure mechanism, and stress incontinence is common afterwards and usually improves over the following months with pelvic floor muscle training, although it can persist and needs assessment if it does. Training helps at any age: squeeze as if stopping the flow of urine and holding back wind, hold, relax and repeat, NICE advising at least eight contractions three times a day for at least three months. After vaginoplasty the neovagina lies within the levator ani, and pelvic floor physiotherapy to relax the muscles makes dilation easier.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Weakness of the pelvic floor underlies two very common problems. Stress urinary incontinence is leakage on coughing, laughing or exercise, and pelvic organ prolapse is descent of the bladder, uterus or rectum into the vagina, felt as a dragging heaviness or a bulge; both are common after childbirth and the menopause, and both are treated first with supervised pelvic floor muscle training (at least three months for incontinence and at least sixteen weeks for prolapse in NICE guidance), with pessaries, vaginal oestrogen or surgery for those who need more. Urgency incontinence, a sudden desperate need to pass urine caused by an overactive bladder muscle rather than a weak floor, is managed differently: NICE advises bladder training for at least six weeks before medicines are considered. Faecal incontinence follows sphincter injury at birth or nerve damage; obstetric anal sphincter injury is the term for third and fourth degree tears. An overactive, tight pelvic floor causes pelvic pain, painful sex and difficulty emptying the bladder or bowel, and is treated with relaxation and physiotherapy rather than strengthening. Incontinence, though common, is not a normal part of ageing and should be assessed.

organs.name: Oesophagus
organs.summary: A muscular tube carrying swallowed food from the pharynx to the stomach.

organs.name: Stomach
organs.summary: A muscular bag that churns food with acid and enzymes before releasing it into the duodenum.

article.title: Stomach Anatomy
article.intro: The stomach is a muscular, J-shaped bag in the upper left abdomen that receives food from the oesophagus, churns it with acid and enzymes into a paste called chyme, and releases it in small amounts into the duodenum. Its lining secretes about two litres of gastric juice a day and protects itself with a layer of mucus and bicarbonate.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: Left upper abdomen under the diaphragm, between the oesophagus and duodenum

keyFacts.label: Regions
keyFacts.value: Cardia, fundus, body, antrum, pylorus

keyFacts.label: Capacity
keyFacts.value: About 50 mL empty, 1-1.5 L after a meal, up to 4 L

keyFacts.label: Secretions
keyFacts.value: Hydrochloric acid, pepsinogen, intrinsic factor, mucus, gastrin, ghrelin

keyFacts.label: Blood supply
keyFacts.value: Branches of the coeliac trunk: left and right gastric, gastro-epiploic and short gastric arteries

keyFacts.label: Nerve supply
keyFacts.value: Vagus nerves (secretion, motility) and sympathetic fibres from the coeliac plexus

sections.heading: Location and relations
sections.body: The stomach lies in the left hypochondrium and epigastrium, below the diaphragm and the left lobe of the liver, in front of the pancreas, spleen and left kidney. Its lesser curvature faces the liver and its greater curvature carries the apron-like greater omentum. The lower oesophageal sphincter at the cardia stops acid refluxing upward; the pyloric sphincter at the outlet controls emptying into the duodenum.

sections.heading: Regions
sections.body: The cardia surrounds the oesophageal opening; the fundus is the dome that rises above it, often full of swallowed air; the body is the main reservoir; the antrum grinds food against the closed pylorus and releases the hormone gastrin; and the pylorus is the thick muscular outlet. Ulcers favour the lesser curvature and the antrum; the fundus and body carry the acid-secreting glands.

sections.heading: Wall and lining
sections.body: Three layers of smooth muscle (an extra oblique layer inside the usual circular and longitudinal coats) let the stomach churn as well as squeeze. The mucosa is thrown into folds (rugae) that flatten as it fills and is packed with gastric pits leading to glands: parietal cells make hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor (needed to absorb vitamin B12), chief cells make pepsinogen, and mucous cells coat the surface with alkaline mucus. Proton pump inhibitors shut down the acid pump in the parietal cells.

sections.heading: Blood supply
sections.body: All of the stomach's arteries come from the coeliac trunk: the left gastric runs along the lesser curvature to meet the right gastric from the hepatic artery, the right and left gastro-epiploic arteries run along the greater curvature, and short gastric arteries from the splenic artery reach the fundus. This rich supply is why bleeding ulcers can be life-threatening, and why the stomach can be reshaped in surgery without losing its blood supply.

sections.heading: Venous drainage
sections.body: Gastric veins accompany the arteries and drain into the portal vein, so stomach blood reaches the liver first. In cirrhosis, veins around the cardia enlarge into varices that can rupture.

sections.heading: Innervation
sections.body: The anterior and posterior vagal trunks enter the abdomen on the oesophagus and supply the stomach: they trigger acid secretion in anticipation of food and drive the peristaltic waves that mix and empty it. Sympathetic fibres reduce motility and carry pain, which is felt in the epigastrium.

sections.heading: Function
sections.body: The stomach stores a meal, kills most swallowed microbes with acid at pH 1-2, begins protein digestion with pepsin, mixes everything into chyme and meters it into the duodenum at a rate the small intestine can handle, roughly 2-4 hours for a mixed meal. It signals hunger with ghrelin and fullness through stretch receptors.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Acid reflux irritates the oesophagus when the lower sphincter fails; Helicobacter pylori infection and anti-inflammatory drugs breach the mucus barrier and cause gastritis and peptic ulcers; stomach cancer arises from the lining. A gastroscopy passes a camera through the cardia to inspect every region and take biopsies.
