organs.name: Small intestine
organs.summary: Duodenum, jejunum and ileum: about six metres where most digestion and absorption happens.

organs.name: Large intestine
organs.summary: Caecum, appendix, colon and rectum absorb water and form stool.

article.title: Large Intestine Anatomy
article.intro: The large intestine is the last 1.5 metres of the gut: the caecum with its appendix, the ascending, transverse, descending and sigmoid colon, the rectum and the anal canal. It absorbs water and salts from the liquid residue arriving from the small intestine, hosts trillions of bacteria, and stores and expels the stool.

keyFacts.label: Length
keyFacts.value: About 1.5 m, 6-7 cm wide at the caecum narrowing to 2.5 cm at the sigmoid

keyFacts.label: Parts
keyFacts.value: Caecum and appendix, ascending, transverse, descending and sigmoid colon, rectum, anal canal

keyFacts.label: Blood supply
keyFacts.value: Superior mesenteric artery to the caecum, ascending and most of the transverse colon; inferior mesenteric artery to the rest

keyFacts.label: Nerve supply
keyFacts.value: Vagus as far as the transverse colon, pelvic parasympathetic nerves beyond; sympathetic fibres from the mesenteric plexuses

keyFacts.label: Transit time
keyFacts.value: About 12-48 hours

keyFacts.label: Water absorbed
keyFacts.value: About 1-1.5 L a day, leaving 100-200 g of stool

sections.heading: Caecum and appendix
sections.body: The ileum opens into the caecum in the right lower abdomen through the ileocaecal valve, which stops contents flowing backwards. The appendix, a blind tube 5-10 cm long, hangs from the caecum; its position varies, most often behind the caecum, which is why appendicitis can present in unusual ways. Its wall is rich in lymphoid tissue.

sections.heading: Colon
sections.body: The ascending colon runs up the right side to the hepatic flexure under the liver, the transverse colon hangs across the abdomen on its own mesentery to the splenic flexure, and the descending colon runs down the left side to become the S-shaped sigmoid colon in the pelvis. The colon's outer muscle is gathered into three bands (taeniae coli) that pucker it into pouches (haustra) and carry fatty tags (appendices epiploicae). The lining has no villi; it is a smooth mucosa packed with mucus-secreting glands.

sections.heading: Rectum and anal canal
sections.body: The rectum follows the curve of the sacrum, storing stool until defecation, and passes through the pelvic floor into the anal canal, closed by an involuntary internal sphincter of smooth muscle and a voluntary external sphincter of skeletal muscle. Stretch of the rectum triggers the urge to defecate; the sphincters and the puborectalis muscle allow it to be deferred.

sections.heading: Blood supply
sections.body: The superior mesenteric artery supplies the caecum, ascending colon and two-thirds of the transverse colon through the ileocolic, right colic and middle colic arteries; the inferior mesenteric artery supplies the rest through the left colic, sigmoid and superior rectal arteries. The marginal artery runs along the whole colon linking the two systems. The splenic flexure, at the junction of the two supplies, is the part most vulnerable when blood flow falls.

sections.heading: Venous drainage
sections.body: Veins mirror the arteries and drain into the portal vein, so colonic cancers spread first to the liver. The lower rectum and anal canal drain into systemic veins as well, so cancers there can spread to the lungs, and the connection between the two systems forms haemorrhoids when pressure rises.

sections.heading: Innervation
sections.body: Parasympathetic fibres (vagus for the proximal colon, pelvic splanchnic nerves from S2-S4 for the descending colon and rectum) drive peristalsis and secretion; sympathetic fibres slow the gut and carry pain. Because pain from the gut is referred to the midline, appendicitis begins as vague pain around the navel and only moves to the right lower abdomen when the inflamed appendix touches the parietal peritoneum.

sections.heading: Function
sections.body: The colon absorbs water and sodium, converting about 1.5 litres of liquid chyme into formed stool. Its bacteria ferment undigested fibre into short-chain fatty acids that feed the lining, make vitamin K and some B vitamins, and shape the immune system. Mass movements a few times a day propel contents into the rectum.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Bowel cancer, most often in the rectum and sigmoid, arises from polyps that a colonoscopy can remove; screening uses a stool test for hidden blood. Ulcerative colitis inflames the rectum and colon, Crohn's disease any part of the gut. Diverticula form in the sigmoid where pressure is highest. Appendicitis is the commonest surgical emergency.

references.title: NIH NIDDK: Your digestive system and how it works

organs.name: Liver
organs.summary: The body's chemical factory: it processes nutrients, detoxifies blood and makes bile. Modelled as eight hepatovenous segments with the biliary tree.

article.title: Liver Anatomy
article.intro: The liver is the largest internal organ, about 1.5 kg of chemical factory tucked under the right ribs. It receives nutrient-rich blood from the gut through the portal vein, processes and stores what the body needs, neutralises toxins, makes bile and most of the proteins in the blood, and can regenerate after losing more than half its mass.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: Right upper abdomen under the diaphragm, protected by ribs 7-11

keyFacts.label: Weight
keyFacts.value: About 1.4-1.6 kg

keyFacts.label: Lobes
keyFacts.value: Right and left (with the small caudate and quadrate lobes); eight functional Couinaud segments

keyFacts.label: Blood supply
keyFacts.value: Hepatic portal vein (75%) and hepatic artery (25%), about 1.5 L/min

keyFacts.label: Drainage
keyFacts.value: Hepatic veins to the inferior vena cava; bile through the hepatic ducts

keyFacts.label: Cells
keyFacts.value: Hepatocytes arranged in plates around sinusoids; Kupffer cells filter the blood

sections.heading: Location and surfaces
sections.body: The liver lies against the underside of the diaphragm, mostly behind the right lower ribs, its left lobe reaching across to the stomach. Its smooth diaphragmatic surface is covered by peritoneum except for a bare area against the diaphragm; its visceral surface is moulded by the gallbladder, duodenum, right kidney and colon. The falciform ligament attaches it to the front abdominal wall and marks the boundary between the anatomical right and left lobes.

sections.heading: Lobes and segments
sections.body: For surgery the liver is divided into eight Couinaud segments, each with its own branch of the portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct, separated by planes that contain the hepatic veins. Segments II-IV form the functional left liver and V-VIII the right; segment I is the caudate lobe, which drains straight into the vena cava. A surgeon can remove any segment or group of segments along these planes with little bleeding and no loss of function in the remainder.

sections.heading: The porta hepatis and bile ducts
sections.body: The portal vein, hepatic artery and common hepatic duct enter and leave the liver at the porta hepatis on its underside, wrapped together in the hepatoduodenal ligament. Bile made by hepatocytes flows through tiny canaliculi into ductules and then the right and left hepatic ducts, which join as the common hepatic duct; the cystic duct from the gallbladder joins it to form the common bile duct, which opens into the duodenum beside the pancreatic duct.

sections.heading: Blood supply
sections.body: Uniquely, most of the liver's blood is venous: the hepatic portal vein brings blood that has already passed through the stomach, intestines, pancreas and spleen, loaded with absorbed nutrients, gut hormones and anything else taken by mouth, including drugs and toxins. The hepatic artery, a branch of the coeliac trunk, brings oxygenated blood. Both mix in the sinusoids between plates of hepatocytes. Because everything absorbed from the gut passes through the liver first, oral drugs can be partly destroyed before reaching the circulation (the first-pass effect).

sections.heading: Venous drainage
sections.body: Blood leaves through three hepatic veins that open into the inferior vena cava just below the diaphragm. When the liver is scarred by cirrhosis, resistance rises, pressure backs up in the portal system, and blood finds alternative routes through veins around the oesophagus and stomach, which can bleed catastrophically.

sections.heading: Innervation
sections.body: Sympathetic fibres from the coeliac plexus and parasympathetic fibres from the vagus reach the liver along its vessels. The liver's own tissue is insensitive to pain; the ache of a swollen liver comes from stretch of its capsule and the overlying peritoneum, and is often felt at the right shoulder because the phrenic nerve shares spinal segments with the shoulder skin.

sections.heading: Function
sections.body: The liver stores glucose as glycogen and releases it between meals, makes new glucose from amino acids, builds plasma proteins including albumin and the clotting factors, manufactures cholesterol and bile salts, stores iron and vitamins A, D and B12, breaks down worn-out red cells into bilirubin, converts ammonia to urea, and inactivates hormones, alcohol and most drugs through its cytochrome enzymes.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Fatty liver, alcohol and viral hepatitis inflame and eventually scar the liver; cirrhosis blocks portal flow and cripples synthesis, so patients bleed, swell with ascites and become jaundiced and confused. Liver function tests read these processes in the blood. Gallstones can block the common bile duct, causing jaundice and pancreatitis. The liver is the commonest site for cancer to spread through the portal vein from the bowel. Paracetamol overdose destroys hepatocytes within days.

organs.name: Gallbladder & bile ducts
organs.summary: Stores and concentrates bile, releasing it into the duodenum through the cystic and common bile ducts.

organs.name: Pancreas
organs.summary: Makes digestive enzymes and the hormones insulin and glucagon.

article.title: Pancreas Anatomy
article.intro: The pancreas is a soft, elongated gland about 15 cm long lying across the back of the upper abdomen behind the stomach. It is two organs in one: exocrine tissue that pours digestive enzymes into the duodenum, and scattered islets that release insulin and glucagon into the blood to control glucose.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: Retroperitoneal, across L1-L2, head in the curve of the duodenum, tail reaching the spleen

keyFacts.label: Parts
keyFacts.value: Head (with uncinate process), neck, body, tail

keyFacts.label: Ducts
keyFacts.value: Main pancreatic duct joining the common bile duct at the ampulla; accessory duct

keyFacts.label: Exocrine output
keyFacts.value: About 1.5 L of alkaline enzyme-rich juice a day

keyFacts.label: Endocrine cells
keyFacts.value: About a million islets of Langerhans: beta cells (insulin), alpha cells (glucagon), delta cells (somatostatin)

keyFacts.label: Blood supply
keyFacts.value: Pancreaticoduodenal arteries and branches of the splenic artery

sections.heading: Location and relations
sections.body: The pancreas lies behind the peritoneum of the lesser sac, with the stomach in front of it and the aorta, inferior vena cava, left kidney and spine behind. Its head nestles in the C-shaped curve of the duodenum, the neck lies over the superior mesenteric vessels, and the tail reaches the hilum of the spleen. Being so deep, the pancreas is hard to examine and its disease often presents late; its pain radiates through to the back.

sections.heading: Ducts
sections.body: The main pancreatic duct runs the length of the gland collecting from lobular ducts and, in most people, joins the common bile duct to open into the duodenum at the major papilla, guarded by the sphincter of Oddi. A gallstone lodging here blocks both ducts, causing jaundice and pancreatitis. The smaller accessory duct opens separately a little higher.

sections.heading: Exocrine tissue
sections.body: Acinar cells make inactive enzyme precursors (trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, lipase, amylase) and duct cells add bicarbonate-rich fluid that neutralises stomach acid. The enzymes are only activated in the duodenum, a safeguard that fails in pancreatitis, when the gland digests itself.

sections.heading: Islets
sections.body: Islets of Langerhans, more numerous in the tail, sense blood glucose directly. Beta cells release insulin after meals so that muscle, fat and liver take up glucose; alpha cells release glucagon between meals to mobilise it. Autoimmune destruction of beta cells causes type 1 diabetes; resistance to insulin with failing beta-cell reserve causes type 2.

sections.heading: Blood supply
sections.body: The head is supplied by the superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries from the gastroduodenal artery and the inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries from the superior mesenteric artery, which form arcades shared with the duodenum, so the two cannot be separated in surgery (the Whipple operation removes both). The body and tail receive branches from the splenic artery as it runs along the upper border. Veins drain to the splenic and superior mesenteric veins and thus the portal vein.

sections.heading: Innervation
sections.body: Vagal fibres stimulate secretion; sympathetic fibres from the coeliac and superior mesenteric plexuses carry pain to T6-T10, which is why pancreatic pain bores through to the mid-back. Coeliac plexus block is used to relieve pain in pancreatic cancer.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Acute pancreatitis, usually from gallstones or alcohol, causes severe upper abdominal pain and a raised blood lipase or amylase. Chronic pancreatitis destroys both functions, causing diabetes and fatty stools. Pancreatic cancer in the head presents with painless jaundice from bile duct obstruction. Blood glucose and HbA1c measure the islets' work.

organs.name: Spleen
organs.summary: Filters blood, recycles red cells and houses immune cells.

organs.name: Kidneys
organs.summary: Paired filters that clean the blood and regulate fluid and salts.

article.title: Kidney Anatomy
article.intro: The two kidneys are bean-shaped organs the size of a fist, lying against the back wall of the abdomen on either side of the spine. Each contains about a million nephrons that filter the entire blood volume some sixty times a day, keeping water, salts and acid in balance and clearing waste into the urine.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: Retroperitoneal, T12-L3, the right kidney slightly lower because of the liver

keyFacts.label: Size
keyFacts.value: About 11 cm long, 150 g each

keyFacts.label: Working units
keyFacts.value: About one million nephrons per kidney

keyFacts.label: Blood flow
keyFacts.value: Around 1.2 L/min, a fifth of cardiac output

keyFacts.label: Filtration
keyFacts.value: About 180 L of filtrate a day, 99% reabsorbed

keyFacts.label: Hormones
keyFacts.value: Renin, erythropoietin, active vitamin D

sections.heading: Location and coverings
sections.body: The kidneys lie behind the peritoneum against the psoas and quadratus lumborum muscles, the upper poles tucked under the eleventh and twelfth ribs, with the adrenal gland capping each. A tough fibrous capsule, a layer of perirenal fat and the renal fascia hold them in place and cushion them. Because they sit so far back, kidney pain is felt in the loin and can be tested by tapping the renal angle between the last rib and the spine.

sections.heading: Internal structure
sections.body: A cut kidney shows an outer cortex and inner medulla arranged as renal pyramids, whose tips (papillae) drip urine into cup-shaped minor calyces. These join into major calyces and then the renal pelvis, the funnel that narrows into the ureter at the hilum, where the renal artery enters and the renal vein leaves. Stones formed in the calyces cause agonising pain as they pass into the ureter.

sections.heading: The nephron
sections.body: Each nephron begins with a glomerulus, a tuft of capillaries inside Bowman's capsule, where blood pressure forces water and small solutes through a filter that holds back cells and proteins. The filtrate then passes along the proximal tubule (bulk reabsorption of water, glucose, salts), the loop of Henle dipping into the medulla (creating the salt gradient that lets urine be concentrated), the distal tubule and the collecting duct, where hormones fine-tune how much water and salt is returned to the blood. Diuretics such as furosemide act on the loop; ACE inhibitors lower the pressure in the glomerulus.

sections.heading: Blood supply
sections.body: Each renal artery arises directly from the abdominal aorta and divides into segmental, interlobar, arcuate and interlobular arteries before feeding the glomeruli through afferent arterioles. Blood leaves the glomerulus by an efferent arteriole into a second capillary network around the tubules, then into the renal vein and inferior vena cava. Narrowing of a renal artery drives up blood pressure through renin release.

sections.heading: Innervation
sections.body: Sympathetic nerves from the renal plexus constrict the renal vessels and stimulate renin; there is little parasympathetic supply. Pain from a stone is carried with the sympathetic fibres to spinal segments T11-L2 and referred along the loin, groin and, in men, the testis.

sections.heading: Function
sections.body: The kidneys hold the composition of the blood steady: they excrete urea, creatinine and drugs, regulate sodium, potassium, calcium and phosphate, correct acid-base balance by excreting acid and regenerating bicarbonate, and adjust water excretion under antidiuretic hormone so that blood concentration stays within one or two per cent. They release renin to control blood pressure, erythropoietin to drive red cell production, and activate vitamin D for the bones.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Diabetes and high blood pressure slowly damage the glomeruli, leaking protein into the urine and lowering the filtration rate: chronic kidney disease. Sudden injury from dehydration, sepsis or drugs shows as a rising creatinine. Stones, infection and obstruction affect the collecting system. When function falls below about a tenth, dialysis or a transplant replaces the filtering.

references.title: NIH NIDDK: Your kidneys and how they work

organs.name: Adrenal glands
organs.summary: Glands on top of each kidney producing cortisol, aldosterone and adrenaline.

organs.name: Urinary bladder & urethra
organs.summary: The bladder stores urine; the urethra carries it out of the body.

organs.name: Ureters
organs.summary: Muscular tubes carrying urine from the kidneys to the bladder.

organs.name: Prostate
organs.summary: A walnut-sized gland below the bladder that adds fluid to semen.

organs.name: Testes & epididymis
organs.summary: The testes produce sperm and testosterone; the epididymis stores maturing sperm.

organs.name: Penis
organs.summary: Erectile bodies (corpora cavernosa and spongiosum) and the glans.

organs.name: Uterus & cervix
organs.summary: The womb: a pear-sized muscular organ behind the bladder whose lining is shed each month or supports a pregnancy; the cervix is its neck, opening into the vagina.

article.title: Uterus Anatomy
article.intro: The uterus is a hollow, thick-walled, pear-shaped muscular organ about 7.5 cm long that lies in the pelvis between the bladder and the rectum. Its lining is shed each month as a period, it houses and nourishes a pregnancy while growing to many times its resting size, and its muscle delivers the baby at birth.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: In the pelvis behind the bladder and in front of the rectum, usually tilted and bent forward (anteverted and anteflexed)

keyFacts.label: Size
keyFacts.value: About 7.5 cm long, 5 cm wide and 2.5 cm thick in someone who has not been pregnant; about a kilogram by the end of pregnancy

keyFacts.label: Parts
keyFacts.value: Fundus, body, isthmus and cervix; the endocervical canal runs from the internal os to the external os

keyFacts.label: Layers
keyFacts.value: Endometrium (functional layer shed monthly over a basal layer), myometrium (smooth muscle), perimetrium (peritoneum)

keyFacts.label: Supports
keyFacts.value: The levator ani muscles of the pelvic floor with the cardinal and uterosacral ligaments; the round and broad ligaments position rather than support it

keyFacts.label: Blood supply
keyFacts.value: Uterine arteries from the internal iliac arteries, anastomosing with the ovarian arteries; each uterine artery crosses above the ureter near the cervix

keyFacts.label: Nerve supply
keyFacts.value: Uterovaginal plexus from the inferior hypogastric plexus; pain is felt in the lower abdomen, lower back and sacrum

sections.heading: Location and relations
sections.body: The uterus lies in the middle of the pelvis with the bladder in front and the rectum behind. Between uterus and rectum the peritoneum dips into the recto-uterine pouch of Douglas, the lowest point of the peritoneal cavity when standing, where blood from a ruptured ectopic pregnancy or pus from pelvic infection collects. Usually the organ is tilted forward over the bladder (anteverted) and bent forward at the cervix (anteflexed); a backward-tilted uterus is a normal variant. It is held up from below by the levator ani muscles of the pelvic floor and at the sides and back by the cardinal and uterosacral ligaments attached to the cervix. The broad ligament is a peritoneal fold carrying the vessels, and the round ligament runs through the inguinal canal to the labium majus, keeping the uterus anteverted. The ureter passes close to the cervix.

sections.heading: Parts and layers
sections.body: Above the openings of the fallopian tubes lies the rounded fundus; below it the body narrows through the isthmus into the cervix, a firm cylinder about 2.5 cm long that projects into the top of the vagina. The endocervical canal runs from the internal os to the external os and is lined by mucus-secreting columnar epithelium, while the outer surface of the cervix is covered by squamous epithelium. Where the two meet, the transformation zone, is where most cervical cancers begin and where the cells for cervical screening are taken. The wall has three layers: the endometrium, whose functional layer thickens each cycle and is shed at menstruation while the basal layer regenerates it; the myometrium, a thick coat of interlacing smooth muscle that forms most of the organ; and the perimetrium, the visceral peritoneum covering the body and fundus.

sections.heading: Blood supply and lymph
sections.body: Each uterine artery arises from the internal iliac artery, runs medially in the base of the broad ligament and crosses above the ureter close to the cervix, remembered as 'water under the bridge' and the reason the ureter is at risk during hysterectomy. It then climbs tortuously up the side of the uterus, sending branches into the myometrium that end as spiral arterioles in the endometrium; constriction of these vessels starts menstruation. Near the tube it joins the ovarian artery, a direct branch of the abdominal aorta, so the uterus has two sources of supply. Veins form a plexus in the broad ligament draining to the internal iliac veins. Lymph from the cervix and body reaches the internal and external iliac nodes, lymph from the fundus follows the ovarian vessels to the para-aortic nodes, and a few vessels run with the round ligament to the groin.

sections.heading: Innervation
sections.body: The uterus is supplied by the uterovaginal plexus, an extension of the inferior hypogastric plexus lying on either side of the cervix. Sympathetic fibres reach it from the lower thoracic and upper lumbar segments through the hypogastric nerves, and parasympathetic fibres from S2 to S4 through the pelvic splanchnic nerves. Pain from the body of the uterus travels with the sympathetic fibres and is felt in the lower abdomen and lower back, whereas pain from the cervix travels with the parasympathetic fibres and is felt over the sacrum and perineum, which is why period pain and labour pain spread to the back. Contractions in labour are driven mainly by hormones rather than nerves, so labour still proceeds after spinal cord injury, and an epidural blocks the pain pathways without stopping the uterus from working.

sections.heading: Function and hormonal control
sections.body: Under oestrogen from the growing follicle the endometrium proliferates, and after ovulation progesterone from the corpus luteum makes it secretory and receptive. If no embryo implants, the corpus luteum fails, hormone levels fall and the functional layer is shed as a period lasting a few days to a week. If fertilisation occurs in the tube, the embryo implants in the endometrium about a week later; its trophoblast makes hCG, the hormone detected by a pregnancy test, which keeps the corpus luteum working until the placenta takes over. Through pregnancy the myometrium grows by hypertrophy and the uterus rises out of the pelvis, reaching the umbilicus at around 20 weeks and the xiphisternum by about 36 weeks. In labour, oxytocin drives contractions in a positive feedback loop while the cervix softens, thins (effaces) and dilates; afterwards the uterus shrinks back over about six weeks.

sections.heading: Changes across life
sections.body: Before puberty the uterus is small and the cervix makes up much of its length; under rising oestrogen at puberty the body grows and the first period (menarche) follows. Pregnancy stretches the myometrium and the cervix, and each birth leaves the organ slightly larger. After the menopause the uterus shrinks, the endometrium becomes thin and periods stop, so any bleeding after the menopause needs prompt assessment. In trans men and non-binary people taking testosterone, periods usually stop within a few months, but bleeding can continue or return, and any unexpected bleeding needs assessment. The uterus stays in place unless a hysterectomy is chosen as part of gender-affirming surgery, sometimes with removal of the ovaries, which brings on a surgical menopause and raises the same bone health questions. Hysterectomy may also be done before phalloplasty, where a vaginectomy is usually needed if the urethra is lengthened. A retained cervix still needs cervical screening, and testosterone is not a contraceptive.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Fibroids, benign smooth-muscle growths of the myometrium, are the commonest uterine tumour and a major cause of heavy periods, which can lead to iron deficiency anaemia. Endometriosis is endometrium-like tissue growing outside the uterus, and adenomyosis is its growth into the myometrium; both cause pelvic pain. Persistent infection with high-risk HPV can turn cells of the transformation zone into cervical cancer. Cervical screening, offered in the UK by invitation between the ages of 25 and 64 to everyone with a cervix, including trans men and non-binary people, is not a test for cancer: it looks for high-risk HPV and for the cell changes that come before cancer, so they can be treated. People registered as male with their GP practice may need to ask for it, and symptoms such as bleeding after sex or after the menopause need examination rather than screening. Weakened supports allow the uterus to prolapse into the vagina. A caesarean section opens the lower segment of the uterus to deliver the baby; hysterectomy removes the uterus for heavy bleeding, fibroids, prolapse or cancer. A pregnancy implanting outside the cavity, usually in the tube, is an ectopic pregnancy and a surgical emergency if it ruptures.

organs.name: Ovaries & fallopian tubes
organs.summary: The female gonads, one on each side of the uterus, release an egg each cycle and make oestrogen and progesterone; the fallopian tubes carry the egg to the uterus and are where fertilisation happens.

article.title: Ovary & Fallopian Tube Anatomy
article.intro: The ovaries are two almond-shaped glands about 3 cm long that lie against the side walls of the pelvis. Each holds a lifetime's supply of eggs, releases one at ovulation in most cycles and makes oestrogen and progesterone, while the fallopian tubes catch the egg, provide the site of fertilisation and carry the embryo to the uterus.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: Ovarian fossa on the lateral pelvic wall, behind the broad ligament, near the external and internal iliac vessels, the ureter and the obturator nerve

keyFacts.label: Size
keyFacts.value: About 3 cm long, 2 cm wide and 1 cm thick; smaller after the menopause

keyFacts.label: Attachments
keyFacts.value: Suspensory ligament carrying the ovarian vessels, ovarian ligament to the uterus, mesovarium to the broad ligament

keyFacts.label: Blood supply
keyFacts.value: Ovarian artery from the abdominal aorta at about L2; the right ovarian vein drains to the inferior vena cava, the left to the left renal vein

keyFacts.label: Fallopian tubes
keyFacts.value: About 10 cm long: infundibulum with fimbriae, ampulla (site of fertilisation), isthmus and intramural part

keyFacts.label: Hormones
keyFacts.value: Oestradiol from granulosa cells, progesterone from the corpus luteum, inhibin, anti-Mullerian hormone and small amounts of testosterone

keyFacts.label: Ovulation
keyFacts.value: One mature follicle releases its oocyte about 14 days before the next period, in response to the LH surge

sections.heading: Location and relations
sections.body: Each ovary lies on the side wall of the pelvis in the ovarian fossa, a shallow depression bounded in front by the external iliac vessels and behind by the internal iliac vessels and the ureter; the obturator nerve runs across its floor, which is why ovarian disease can refer pain to the inner thigh. The ovary hangs from the back of the broad ligament by a short fold, the mesovarium, is tethered to the corner of the uterus by the ovarian ligament, and receives its vessels through the suspensory ligament, a fold of peritoneum descending over the pelvic brim. Unlike most abdominal organs it is not covered by peritoneum, so the oocyte released at ovulation enters the peritoneal cavity and must be caught by the fimbriae of the tube. After pregnancy the ovaries often sit lower and less predictably in the pelvis.

sections.heading: Structure of the ovary
sections.body: A cut ovary shows an outer cortex packed with follicles at every stage and an inner medulla of loose connective tissue, vessels and nerves that enter at the hilum. The surface is a single layer of cuboidal cells over a fibrous tunica albuginea. Primordial follicles, each an oocyte arrested in the first meiotic division and wrapped in a single layer of flat cells, are formed before birth and never replenished: of the million or so present at birth, only a few hundred are ever ovulated. Each cycle a small group is recruited to grow into primary, secondary and then fluid-filled antral follicles; usually one becomes dominant, reaches about 2 cm across and ruptures at ovulation. Its remnant becomes the corpus luteum, a yellow hormone-secreting body that, if no pregnancy follows, regresses over about two weeks into a small scar, the corpus albicans.

sections.heading: The fallopian tubes
sections.body: The two fallopian (uterine) tubes, each about 10 cm long, run in the upper free edge of the broad ligament from the corners of the uterus towards the ovaries. From the outer end inwards each has an infundibulum, a funnel fringed with finger-like fimbriae that drape over the ovary; an ampulla, the widest and longest part, where fertilisation normally takes place and where most ectopic pregnancies implant; a narrow, thick-walled isthmus; and a short intramural part through the wall of the uterus. The folded lining carries ciliated cells that beat towards the uterus and secretory cells that nourish the oocyte and early embryo, while the muscle coat adds gentle peristalsis. Because the tube opens into the peritoneal cavity, infection ascending from the vagina and uterus can spread to the peritoneum, and scarring of the tube after infection is a common cause of infertility.

sections.heading: Blood supply and lymph
sections.body: The ovarian arteries arise from the abdominal aorta just below the renal arteries, at about the level of the second lumbar vertebra, a reminder that the ovary forms high on the back wall of the embryo before descending into the pelvis. Each runs down behind the peritoneum, crosses the pelvic brim in the suspensory ligament and supplies the ovary and tube before joining the ovarian branch of the uterine artery, so the tube is fed from both ends. Venous blood collects in a pampiniform plexus and leaves in the ovarian vein: the right drains directly into the inferior vena cava, the left into the left renal vein. Lymph follows the ovarian vessels upward to the para-aortic nodes beside the aorta and vena cava, which is why ovarian cancer can spread to nodes high in the abdomen and why staging surgery samples them.

sections.heading: Innervation
sections.body: The ovary receives its nerves from the ovarian plexus, which descends around the ovarian artery from the aortic and renal plexuses and carries sympathetic fibres from the tenth and eleventh thoracic segments, with a further contribution from the uterovaginal plexus in the pelvis. Pain from the ovary and tube is therefore felt in the lower abdomen around the T10 and T11 dermatomes rather than at the organ itself: the brief twinge some women notice at ovulation (mittelschmerz) and the sudden severe pain of a twisted or ruptured cyst both present this way, and irritation of the nearby obturator nerve can add pain along the inner thigh. The nerves have little influence on ovulation, which is controlled by hormones from the pituitary gland.

sections.heading: Function and hormonal control
sections.body: The ovary is both the source of eggs and an endocrine gland under the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis. Pulses of GnRH from the hypothalamus make the pituitary release FSH and LH; FSH drives follicle growth, and the granulosa cells of the growing follicle convert androgens made by the neighbouring theca cells into oestradiol. Rising oestradiol first suppresses the pituitary by negative feedback, then at its mid-cycle peak switches to positive feedback and triggers the LH surge that ripens the oocyte and ruptures the follicle. The corpus luteum then secretes progesterone, which prepares the endometrium for implantation and raises basal body temperature; if pregnancy occurs, hCG from the embryo keeps it working until the placenta takes over, otherwise it fails and a period follows. The ovary also makes inhibin, which restrains FSH, anti-Mullerian hormone from small follicles (a marker of egg reserve) and small amounts of testosterone.

sections.heading: Changes across life
sections.body: The ovaries are quiet in childhood and wake at puberty when GnRH pulses begin; oestrogen then drives breast growth, growth of the uterus and the first period. The store of follicles falls steadily through the reproductive years, faster from the mid-thirties, so fertility declines well before periods stop. When too few follicles remain, cycles become irregular (the perimenopause) and cease at the menopause, on average around 51 in the UK; the ovary shrinks, oestrogen falls sharply and bone loss speeds up. Loss of ovarian function before 40 is premature ovarian insufficiency. In trans men and non-binary people taking testosterone, ovulation is not reliably suppressed, so contraception is still needed where pregnancy is possible; the ovaries remain unless removed by oophorectomy, which causes a surgical menopause with the same bone considerations, and egg freezing can be discussed beforehand. Trans women do not have ovaries; where feminising hormone therapy is used, oestrogen is given as a medicine rather than made by a gonad.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Functional cysts form when a follicle or corpus luteum fails to regress; most are painless and disappear within a few cycles, but a large cyst can twist the ovary on its suspensory ligament (torsion) or rupture, causing sudden severe pain that needs urgent assessment. Polycystic ovary syndrome is diagnosed when two of three features are present: irregular or absent ovulation, clinical or biochemical excess androgen, and many small follicles on ultrasound. Scanning is not needed when the other two features are present, and other causes must first be excluded. Ovarian cancer often presents late with persistent bloating, feeling full quickly, pelvic or abdominal pain and urinary frequency, particularly after 50; there is no screening programme, so new, persistent or frequent symptoms should be discussed with a GP, who may arrange a CA125 blood test and, if it is raised, an ultrasound scan. An ectopic pregnancy most often implants in the ampulla of the tube: a positive pregnancy test with one-sided pelvic pain, bleeding, shoulder-tip pain or faintness needs urgent assessment, because a ruptured ectopic pregnancy is an emergency. Pelvic inflammatory disease scars the tubes, raising the risk of ectopic pregnancy and infertility. Endometriosis commonly involves the ovaries as blood-filled 'chocolate cysts'. Before chemotherapy or gender-affirming treatment, eggs can be frozen to preserve fertility.

organs.name: Vagina
organs.summary: A muscular, elastic canal about 8 to 10 cm long from the cervix to the vulva, between the bladder and urethra in front and the rectum behind: the birth canal and the passage for menstrual blood.

article.title: Vagina Anatomy
article.intro: The vagina is a fibromuscular canal about 8 to 10 cm long that runs upwards and backwards from the vulva to the cervix, lying between the bladder and urethra in front and the rectum behind. It carries menstrual blood out of the body, receives the penis and semen during intercourse and stretches to become the birth canal, and its oestrogen-dependent lining keeps itself acidic and largely self-cleaning.

keyFacts.label: Length
keyFacts.value: About 8 to 10 cm; the anterior wall is shorter than the posterior because the cervix enters the upper end at an angle

keyFacts.label: Lining
keyFacts.value: Non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium, rich in glycogen under oestrogen; the vagina has no glands of its own

keyFacts.label: Acidity
keyFacts.value: pH about 3.8 to 4.5 in the reproductive years, maintained by lactobacilli

keyFacts.label: Relations
keyFacts.value: Bladder base and urethra in front, rectum and pouch of Douglas behind, levator ani on each side, perineal body below

keyFacts.label: Blood supply
keyFacts.value: Vaginal branches of the uterine artery, the vaginal artery and branches of the internal pudendal artery

keyFacts.label: Nerve supply
keyFacts.value: Upper part autonomic via the uterovaginal plexus, lower part somatic via the pudendal nerve (S2-S4)

keyFacts.label: Lymph
keyFacts.value: Upper part to the internal and external iliac nodes, lowest part to the superficial inguinal nodes

sections.heading: Location and relations
sections.body: The vagina runs upwards and backwards from its opening in the vestibule of the vulva to the cervix, which projects into its upper end. The recess around the cervix is the fornix, with anterior, posterior and two lateral parts; the posterior fornix is the deepest and is separated by only a thin wall from the rectouterine pouch (pouch of Douglas), so fluid collecting in the pelvis can be felt or drained through it. In front lie the base of the bladder and the urethra, embedded in the anterior vaginal wall. Behind lie the pouch of Douglas above, the rectum in the middle and the perineal body below, which separates the lower vagina from the anal canal. The levator ani muscles hug the canal on each side, and the ureters pass close to the lateral fornices, where they are at risk in pelvic surgery.

sections.heading: Structure and layers
sections.body: The wall has four layers. The lining is a non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium that thickens and stores glycogen under oestrogen; the vagina has no glands of its own, and its moisture comes from fluid seeping through the wall, cervical mucus and the vestibular glands at the opening. Beneath it the lamina propria carries a dense venous plexus, then a muscularis of inner circular and outer longitudinal smooth muscle, and an outer adventitia that blends with the pelvic fascia. Transverse ridges called rugae let the canal distend in intercourse and childbirth. At the opening the hymen, a thin fold of mucosa of very variable shape, partly narrows the entrance in early life; it stretches or tears with tampon use, exercise or intercourse, and small remnants persist in adults. Its appearance varies widely and is not a reliable indication of whether a person has had sex. Lactobacilli ferment the glycogen of shed epithelial cells into lactic acid, producing the acidity that restrains other organisms.

sections.heading: Blood supply and lymph
sections.body: Arterial blood comes from branches of the internal iliac artery: vaginal branches of the uterine artery to the upper part, the vaginal artery (from the internal iliac or the uterine artery) to the middle, and branches of the internal pudendal and middle rectal arteries to the lower part. Their anastomoses form longitudinal channels, the azygos arteries, on the anterior and posterior walls. Blood drains into a vaginal venous plexus in the lamina propria that joins the uterine plexus and empties into the internal iliac veins. Lymph from the upper vagina drains, like that of the cervix, to the internal and external iliac nodes; lymph from the lowest part, below the hymen, drains with the vulva to the superficial inguinal nodes in the groin. The split matters in cancer staging: a tumour of the lower vagina spreads to the groin nodes, one of the upper vagina into the pelvis.

sections.heading: Innervation
sections.body: The upper three-quarters of the vagina are supplied by autonomic fibres from the uterovaginal plexus, with sympathetic fibres from the lower thoracic and upper lumbar cord and parasympathetic fibres from the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4). This part is sensitive to stretch but poorly sensitive to touch and temperature, which is why a speculum or a pessary high in the vagina is felt as pressure rather than touch. The lowest part, near the opening, is supplied by the somatic pudendal nerve (S2-S4) through its deep perineal branch and is richly sensitive to touch, pain and temperature. A pudendal nerve block therefore numbs the lower vagina and perineum for an instrumental delivery or the repair of a tear, whereas labour pain from the cervix and upper vagina travels with the autonomic fibres and is felt deep in the pelvis and low back.

sections.heading: Function
sections.body: The vagina has four main roles. It carries menstrual blood and cervical mucus out of the body; the discharge changes through the cycle, becoming clear and stretchy around ovulation. During sexual arousal its walls lubricate with fluid transuded through the epithelium, the upper part lengthens and widens, and the lower third and the vestibule carry most of the sensation; semen is deposited near the cervix. In labour it stretches to several times its resting width to form the birth canal, the rugae flattening out, and recovers over the following weeks. Throughout the reproductive years it maintains its own microbiome: oestrogen drives glycogen into the epithelial cells, shed cells feed lactobacilli, and the lactic acid they make keeps the pH at about 3.8 to 4.5, which suppresses many bacteria and yeasts. Douching and scented washes disturb this balance and are not needed; the vagina cleans itself.

sections.heading: Changes across life
sections.body: The lining depends on oestrogen. Before puberty the epithelium is thin, the pH near neutral and lactobacilli sparse; at puberty the epithelium thickens, glycogen accumulates, the pH falls and a physiological discharge begins. Pregnancy increases blood flow and softens the tissues, and vaginal birth stretches the canal and perineum; tears are graded from first degree (skin and vaginal lining) through second (perineal muscles) to third and fourth degree, which reach the anal sphincter and anal lining. After the menopause the loss of oestrogen thins the epithelium, reduces lactobacilli and raises the pH, causing dryness, soreness, painful sex, urinary symptoms and recurrent urinary tract infections: the genitourinary syndrome of menopause, which vaginal oestrogen relieves. Trans men and non-binary people taking testosterone can develop similar atrophy, because the therapy suppresses ovarian oestrogen production, and topical vaginal oestrogen can be used alongside testosterone without reversing masculinising effects. Vaginoplasty, carried out for trans women and some non-binary people and also for congenital absence of the vagina, constructs a neovagina from penile and scrotal skin, peritoneum or bowel; a skin-lined canal does not self-lubricate or carry the same flora, and it needs a lifelong dilation routine.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Thrush is an overgrowth of Candida causing itch and a thick white discharge; bacterial vaginosis is a shift away from lactobacilli that raises the pH and produces a thin, fishy-smelling discharge. Weakness of the pelvic floor and vaginal walls after childbirth and the menopause lets the bladder bulge into the anterior wall (cystocele), the rectum into the posterior wall (rectocele) or the uterus or vault descend: pelvic organ prolapse, often with urinary incontinence, managed with pelvic floor muscle training, pessaries, vaginal oestrogen or surgery. A fistula between the vagina and the bladder or rectum can follow obstructed labour, surgery or radiotherapy and causes continuous leakage. Vaginal oestrogen may also be considered after the menopause for women, and anyone with a vagina, who have recurrent urinary tract infections. The vagina is also the route for speculum examination and cervical screening, transvaginal ultrasound, vaginal hysterectomy and prolapse repair. Vaginal cancer is rare, but bleeding after sex or after the menopause always needs examination.

organs.name: Vulva & clitoris
organs.summary: The external female genitalia: the mons pubis, labia majora and minora, the clitoris, the vestibule with the urethral and vaginal openings, and the glands that open into it.

article.title: Vulva & Clitoris Anatomy
article.intro: The vulva is the external genitalia: the mons pubis, the labia majora and minora, the clitoris, the vestibule into which the urethra and vagina open, and the glands around them, resting on the front of the perineum between the thighs. Its centrepiece, the clitoris, is a densely innervated erectile organ homologous with the penis, most of which lies beneath the surface.

keyFacts.label: Parts
keyFacts.value: Mons pubis, labia majora, labia minora, clitoris, vestibule, Bartholin's and Skene's glands

keyFacts.label: Clitoris
keyFacts.value: Glans, body, two crura and two vestibular bulbs of erectile tissue, most of it beneath the surface

keyFacts.label: Openings
keyFacts.value: Urethral meatus in front and vaginal opening behind, both within the vestibule

keyFacts.label: Blood supply
keyFacts.value: Internal pudendal artery, with external pudendal branches from the femoral artery to the mons and front of the labia

keyFacts.label: Nerve supply
keyFacts.value: Pudendal nerve (S2-S4), with ilioinguinal and genitofemoral branches to the mons and anterior labia

keyFacts.label: Lymph
keyFacts.value: Superficial inguinal nodes in the groin

keyFacts.label: Development
keyFacts.value: From the same genital tubercle, folds and swellings that form the penis and scrotum

sections.heading: Location and relations
sections.body: The vulva occupies the front of the perineum, the diamond-shaped region between the thighs bounded by the pubic symphysis in front, the ischial tuberosities at the sides and the coccyx behind; the urogenital triangle in front holds the vulva, the anal triangle behind holds the anal canal and its external sphincter. The mons pubis is the fat pad over the symphysis, and the labia extend back from it to the perineal body, the fibromuscular knot between the vaginal opening and the anus into which the pelvic floor and perineal muscles insert. Beneath the skin lie the crura of the clitoris on the ischiopubic rami and the vestibular bulbs beside the vaginal opening, covered by the ischiocavernosus and bulbospongiosus muscles. The short female urethra, about 4 cm long, opens into the vestibule just in front of the vagina, one reason urinary tract infections are common in women.

sections.heading: Structure
sections.body: The labia majora are two hair-bearing folds of skin and fat, meeting in front at the mons and behind near the perineal body. Within them lie the labia minora, thin hairless folds rich in sebaceous glands, vessels and nerve endings; in front each splits to form the prepuce (hood) over the glans of the clitoris and the frenulum beneath it, and behind they join at the fourchette. The clitoris has a glans, a short body, two crura along the ischiopubic rami and two vestibular bulbs flanking the vaginal opening, all erectile tissue that swells with blood during arousal; only the glans is visible, and most of the organ lies beneath the surface. The vestibule between the labia minora holds the urethral meatus, the vaginal opening, the ducts of Skene's (paraurethral) glands beside the urethra and the openings of Bartholin's (greater vestibular) glands on either side of the lower part of the vaginal opening.

sections.heading: Blood supply and lymph
sections.body: Most of the vulva is supplied by the internal pudendal artery, a branch of the internal iliac that reaches the perineum by passing round the ischial spine and gives the perineal and posterior labial arteries, the artery of the bulb and the deep and dorsal arteries of the clitoris. The mons and the front of the labia receive external pudendal branches from the femoral artery. Venous blood returns through the internal pudendal veins and, from the clitoris, through the deep dorsal vein into the venous plexus around the bladder. The vestibular bulbs are so vascular that a straddle injury or a difficult birth can produce a large vulval haematoma. Lymph drains to the superficial inguinal nodes in the groin and then to the deep inguinal and external iliac nodes, which is why vulval cancer is staged by assessing the groin nodes and a vulval infection causes tender groin glands.

sections.heading: Innervation
sections.body: The pudendal nerve (S2-S4) supplies most of the vulva. It gives perineal branches carrying the posterior labial nerves to the labia and vestibule, and the dorsal nerve of the clitoris, which makes the glans densely innervated and the most sensitive part of the genitalia. The mons and the front of the labia majora are supplied by the ilioinguinal nerve and the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve (L1-L2), the back of the labia by the perineal branch of the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve. Autonomic fibres from the uterovaginal plexus reach the erectile tissue through the cavernous nerves and produce engorgement during arousal. A pudendal nerve block at the ischial spine anaesthetises the vulva and lower vagina for an instrumental birth or the repair of a tear, and in phalloplasty the dorsal nerve of the clitoris is joined to the nerve of the flap to give the neophallus sensation.

sections.heading: Function and development
sections.body: The vulva protects the openings of the urethra and vagina and carries most of the sensation of the female genitalia. In arousal the clitoris and bulbs fill with blood, the labia swell and darken and the Bartholin's glands secrete mucus; the clitoris has no part in urination or reproduction, and its role is sensation and arousal. In the embryo the external genitalia of both sexes begin as the same genital tubercle, urogenital folds and labioscrotal swellings: without androgens the tubercle becomes the clitoris, the folds the labia minora and the swellings the labia majora, whereas testosterone and dihydrotestosterone turn the same tissues into the penis, penile urethra and scrotum, and the Bartholin's and Skene's glands correspond to the bulbourethral glands and prostate. These homologies underlie gender-affirming surgery: vaginoplasty fashions the glans of the penis into a neoclitoris, and metoidioplasty releases the enlarged clitoris to form a small phallus.

sections.heading: Changes across life
sections.body: In childhood the labia majora are thin and hairless and the labia minora small. At puberty adrenal androgens bring pubic hair, and oestrogen deposits fat in the mons and labia majora, enlarges and darkens the labia minora and activates the glands. Pregnancy increases the blood supply, and vaginal birth stretches the vulva and perineum, where tears and episiotomies heal. After the menopause the loss of oestrogen thins the skin of the labia and vestibule, reduces labial fat and pubic hair, and causes dryness, itching and soreness: the genitourinary syndrome of menopause, which vaginal oestrogen relieves. Testosterone therapy in trans men and non-binary people enlarges the clitoris over months, typically to a few centimetres, a change that metoidioplasty makes use of. In trans women and some non-binary people, vaginoplasty constructs the labia from scrotal and penile skin and a neoclitoris from the glans of the penis, keeping its nerves and vessels.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: A blocked Bartholin's gland forms a cyst beside the lower part of the vaginal opening; a small one often causes no symptoms, while a larger one feels uncomfortable, and an infected gland forms an abscess that is very painful and may need draining. Lichen sclerosus, a chronic inflammatory skin condition, causes itch, white thinned skin and scarring; it is treated with steroid ointment and is kept under review, because a small number of people with it go on to develop vulval cancer, which is rare and presents as a persistent lump, ulcer, itch or bleeding needing examination. Vulvodynia is persistent vulval pain with no visible cause; thrush, herpes and genital warts affect the vulval skin and are managed in sexual health clinics. Female genital mutilation, the cutting or removal of vulval tissue for non-medical reasons, is illegal in the UK and causes pain, scarring, urinary and menstrual problems, difficult childbirth and lasting psychological harm; specialist clinics offer support and deinfibulation where the opening has been narrowed. Wide variation in the size and shape of the labia is normal.

organs.name: Breasts
organs.summary: Modified sweat glands on the front of the chest wall over pectoralis major: 15 to 20 lobes of milk-producing tissue draining to the nipple, in fat and supporting ligaments, with lymph drainage mainly to the armpit.

article.title: Breast Anatomy
article.intro: The breasts are paired modified sweat glands on the front of the chest wall, lying over the pectoralis major muscles and made of milk-producing lobes embedded in fat and tethered by fibrous ligaments. They grow under oestrogen and progesterone, make milk under prolactin and release it under oxytocin, and they are the site of the commonest cancer in women.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: On the front of the chest from the 2nd to the 6th rib and from the edge of the sternum to the mid-axillary line, with the axillary tail extending into the armpit

keyFacts.label: Glandular tissue
keyFacts.value: 15 to 20 lobes of branching tubulo-alveolar glands, each draining through a lactiferous duct that widens into a sinus before opening on the nipple

keyFacts.label: Support
keyFacts.value: Fat, and the suspensory ligaments (of Cooper) that run from the skin through the gland to the deep fascia over pectoralis major

keyFacts.label: Blood supply
keyFacts.value: Perforating branches of the internal thoracic artery, the lateral thoracic artery from the axillary artery, and perforating branches of the intercostal arteries

keyFacts.label: Lymph drainage
keyFacts.value: About three-quarters to the axillary nodes, most of the rest to the parasternal (internal mammary) nodes along the internal thoracic vessels

keyFacts.label: Nerve supply
keyFacts.value: Anterior and lateral cutaneous branches of the 4th to 6th intercostal nerves; the nipple lies in the T4 dermatome

keyFacts.label: Hormonal control
keyFacts.value: Oestrogen grows the ducts and fat, progesterone the lobules; prolactin drives milk production and oxytocin milk ejection

sections.heading: Location and relations
sections.body: Each breast lies in the superficial fascia of the front of the chest wall, extending from about the second to the sixth rib and from the lateral edge of the sternum to the mid-axillary line. A tongue of glandular tissue, the axillary tail, runs from the upper outer quadrant along the lower border of pectoralis major towards the armpit, which is why breast tissue and breast lumps can be found in the axilla. About two-thirds of the base rests on the fascia over pectoralis major and the rest on serratus anterior. Between the gland and the pectoral fascia lies the retromammary space, a layer of loose connective tissue that lets the breast move freely over the muscle; a cancer that grows through it fixes the breast to the chest wall. The nipple usually sits at the fourth intercostal space, though its position varies with breast size and age.

sections.heading: Structure: lobes, ducts and the nipple
sections.body: The gland consists of 15 to 20 lobes arranged like the spokes of a wheel around the nipple, each a tubulo-alveolar gland whose lobules of secretory alveoli drain into progressively larger ducts. Every lobe empties through a single lactiferous duct that widens into a lactiferous sinus beneath the areola and then narrows to open on the tip of the nipple. Smooth muscle in the nipple makes it erect with cold, touch or suckling, and the pigmented areola carries the small bumps of the areolar (Montgomery) glands, whose oily secretion protects the skin during breastfeeding. The lobes are embedded in fat, which gives the breast most of its size and shape, and the gland is tethered by the suspensory ligaments of Cooper, fibrous bands running from the skin to the deep fascia. A tumour that shortens these ligaments draws in the skin above it, the dimpling that warns of cancer.

sections.heading: Blood supply and lymph
sections.body: Blood reaches the breast from several directions: perforating branches of the internal thoracic (internal mammary) artery pierce the upper intercostal spaces beside the sternum to supply the medial part, the lateral thoracic artery from the axillary artery supplies the upper and lateral parts, and perforating branches of the posterior intercostal arteries arrive from behind. Veins drain mainly to the axillary and internal thoracic veins. Lymph drainage matters most clinically, because breast cancer spreads along it. About three-quarters of the lymph, especially from the lateral quadrants, passes to the axillary nodes, which surgeons group into three levels around pectoralis minor. Most of the rest drains to the parasternal (internal mammary) nodes along the internal thoracic vessels. Injecting a tracer beside a tumour identifies the first, or sentinel, node it drains to, which can be examined instead of clearing the whole axilla.

sections.heading: Innervation
sections.body: Sensation from the skin of the breast is carried by the anterior and lateral cutaneous branches of the fourth, fifth and sixth intercostal nerves, with the supraclavicular nerves supplying the skin of the upper part. The nipple and areola lie in the fourth thoracic dermatome and are supplied chiefly by the lateral cutaneous branch of the fourth intercostal nerve, so nipple sensation can be reduced or lost if that branch is divided during breast surgery. These nerves also carry sympathetic fibres to the blood vessels and to the smooth muscle of the nipple; the gland itself has no motor supply, because milk secretion is controlled by hormones. Suckling stimulates sensory endings in the nipple and the signal travels to the hypothalamus, releasing prolactin and oxytocin. Surgery in the axilla can injure the intercostobrachial nerve, leaving numbness on the inner side of the upper arm.

sections.heading: Function and hormonal control
sections.body: The purpose of the breast is lactation. During pregnancy, oestrogen, progesterone and placental hormones make the ducts branch and the alveoli multiply, and prolactin from the anterior pituitary rises steadily, but the high sex hormone levels block its action so that little milk is made before birth. Once the placenta is delivered, oestrogen and progesterone fall sharply and prolactin switches on full milk secretion within a few days; the first milk is colostrum, thick and rich in protein and antibodies. Suckling keeps the system going: input from the nipple sustains prolactin release and triggers oxytocin from the posterior pituitary, which contracts the myoepithelial cells around the alveoli and squeezes milk into the ducts, the let-down reflex. Supply follows demand, and the high prolactin of frequent breastfeeding often delays the return of ovulation and periods, though ovulation can return before the first period, so breastfeeding only prevents pregnancy reliably under the strict conditions of the lactational amenorrhoea method: fully breastfeeding, no periods yet returned and the baby under six months.

sections.heading: Changes across life
sections.body: Before puberty, and in men throughout life, the breast is a small system of rudimentary ducts beneath the nipple that hormonal change or some medicines can enlarge (gynaecomastia). At puberty oestrogen grows the ducts and lays down fat, and progesterone develops the lobules once cycles become ovulatory; the lobules swell before each period, causing fullness and tenderness. Pregnancy enlarges the breast, and after the menopause glandular tissue gives way to fat. In trans women, breast growth usually begins about three to six months after starting oestrogen and continues over about two to three years, usually to a smaller size than in cisgender women. Trans women and non-binary people who have taken feminising hormones for several years are eligible for breast screening: those registered as female with a GP are invited in the same way as anyone else on the register, while those registered as male are not invited automatically and can ask their GP or local screening service to arrange it. Trans men who have not had chest surgery are eligible on the same basis and may also need to ask.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Breast cancer is the commonest cancer in women worldwide. It usually starts in the cells lining the ducts or lobules and can spread along the lymphatics to the axillary nodes, so a new lump, dimpled skin, a newly inverted nipple, blood-stained discharge or a lump in the armpit should be assessed promptly; a breast clinic combines examination, imaging and a needle biopsy. In England the NHS breast screening programme invites women, and anyone else registered female with a GP who has breast tissue, from the age of 50 up to their 71st birthday for mammography every three years. Most lumps are benign: fibroadenomas, cysts and fibrocystic change. A blocked duct during breastfeeding can lead to mastitis and, untreated, to an abscess. Breast cancer also occurs in men, though rarely. Chest masculinisation removes most but not all of the breast tissue, so a new lump still needs assessment, and augmentation implants sit over or under pectoralis major.

organs.name: Neovagina
organs.summary: The vagina created by vaginoplasty in gender-affirming surgery: a lined canal between the urethra and prostate in front and the rectum behind, with a clitoris fashioned from the glans; the prostate is kept.

article.title: Neovagina Anatomy
article.intro: A neovagina is a vaginal canal and vulva constructed by vaginoplasty, most often as gender-affirming surgery for trans women and some non-binary people, and occasionally where the vagina is absent from birth or lost to cancer surgery. In the commonest technique the skin of the penis and scrotum lines a canal made between the urethra and prostate in front and the rectum behind, and part of the glans becomes the clitoris. Its skin lining needs lifelong care that differs from that of a vagina developed before birth.

keyFacts.label: Made from
keyFacts.value: Inverted penile skin, usually extended with a scrotal skin graft; alternatives line the canal with peritoneum or a segment of sigmoid colon

keyFacts.label: Position
keyFacts.value: Between the urethra, prostate and bladder in front and the rectum behind, passing through the levator ani

keyFacts.label: Clitoris
keyFacts.value: A reduced glans penis kept alive on its dorsal neurovascular bundle

keyFacts.label: Depth
keyFacts.value: Varies with the donor tissue available; commonly around 10 to 15 cm

keyFacts.label: Retained and removed
keyFacts.value: The prostate and a shortened urethra remain; the testes and most of the erectile tissue are removed

keyFacts.label: Lining
keyFacts.value: Keratinised skin that does not lubricate and lacks the lactobacillus flora of a vagina

keyFacts.label: Maintenance
keyFacts.value: Regular dilation for life to keep depth and width

sections.heading: Location and relations
sections.body: The canal occupies a space that in the pelvis of a person assigned male at birth is only potential: the plane between the prostate and membranous urethra in front and the rectum behind, which the surgeon opens from the perineum and widens by parting the pubococcygeus and puborectalis of each side. Its axis runs upward and backward towards the sacrum, as a vagina developed before birth does. The bladder base lies above and in front of the upper canal, the prostate directly behind the anterior wall, and the rectum and external anal sphincter behind the posterior wall, separated from it by only a thin layer of tissue. The perineal body between the introitus and the anus is rebuilt to support the opening, and the tone of the surrounding pelvic floor affects how comfortable dilation is.

sections.heading: Structure and lining
sections.body: In penile-inversion vaginoplasty the penile skin is separated from the erectile bodies as a tube, turned inside out and drawn into the canal as its lining; a graft of scrotal skin, cleared of hair beforehand, extends the depth when needed. The corpora cavernosa are largely removed, the corpus spongiosum is trimmed around the shortened urethra, and the new meatus opens in the vestibule below the clitoris. Both testes are removed (orchidectomy), which ends sperm production and the testes' output of testosterone, so fertility preservation is discussed beforehand. The glans is reduced to form the neoclitoris; scrotal skin forms the labia majora and urethral or penile skin the labia minora and vestibule. The lining is keratinised skin, not the glycogen-rich epithelium of a vagina, so it does not lubricate with arousal as a vagina does. Peritoneal techniques line the upper canal with peritoneum, intestinal vaginoplasty uses a segment of sigmoid colon that secretes mucus, and a zero-depth vulvoplasty creates the external anatomy without a canal.

sections.heading: Blood supply and lymph
sections.body: The tissues keep the vessels they had as the penis and scrotum. The neoclitoris survives on the dorsal neurovascular bundle, the paired dorsal arteries (branches of the internal pudendal artery), the deep dorsal vein and the dorsal nerves, preserved together on a strip of tissue during the dissection; injury to this pedicle is the main threat to the clitoris. The inverted penile skin is nourished through its base and, once healed, by the surrounding tissue, whereas a scrotal graft has no vessels of its own and must gain capillaries from the canal wall, so packing holds it firmly in place for the first days. Lymph from the canal and vulva drains, as from the penis and scrotum, to the superficial inguinal nodes; the prostate and bladder drain to the internal iliac nodes. An intestinal segment keeps its own mesenteric vessels.

sections.heading: Innervation
sections.body: Sensation comes from the nerves that supplied the penis and perineum. The dorsal nerve of the penis, a branch of the pudendal nerve (S2 to S4), travels with the dorsal vessels to the neoclitoris, so the clitoris keeps tactile and erotic sensation and the ability to orgasm is usually retained. The inverted skin of the canal shares this supply but is less sensitive, as shaft skin was. The prostate and the urethra behind the anterior wall receive autonomic fibres from the inferior hypogastric plexus, and pressure on this region during penetration adds to sexual sensation. The pudendal nerve also supplies the external anal sphincter and perineal skin, and the ilioinguinal and genitofemoral nerves the front of the labia majora. Because nerve regrowth is slow, numbness, altered sensation or hypersensitivity is common in the first months and usually settles.

sections.heading: Function and hormonal influence
sections.body: The neovagina serves receptive penetrative sex and, for many people, a sense of bodily congruence; it has no menstrual or reproductive function, and there is no cervix or uterus above it. Because the lining is skin it does not lubricate with arousal, and lubricant is needed for dilation and sex (services usually advise a water-based product with dilators). A skin-lined canal is not reliably colonised by the lactobacilli that keep a vagina acidic; its flora resemble those of skin and the perineum, so odour or discharge can come from retained debris, granulation tissue or overgrowth of skin and bowel organisms as well as sexually transmitted infections, and persistent discharge, bleeding or pain needs assessment. An intestinal neovagina produces mucus continuously. Oestrogen taken as gender-affirming therapy is usually continued after recovery, although some teams pause it around surgery because of the risk of venous thrombosis. The canal has no monthly cycle.

sections.heading: Changes after surgery and over life
sections.body: Vaginoplasty is one part of gender-affirming care that some, not all, trans women and non-binary people choose; gender incongruence is not a mental illness, and the World Health Organization classifies it under conditions related to sexual health. The canal is most fragile in the first weeks, when the graft is taking and the lining contracting; left unopposed, a skin-lined canal narrows and shortens, so dilation begins once the packing is removed. Schedules vary between services, frequent at first and then reducing to a maintenance routine that continues for life unless regular penetrative sex maintains depth. Rinsing removes debris, and pelvic floor physiotherapy helps those who find dilation painful because the levator ani tightens. Over the years, hair can grow in the canal if the donor skin was not cleared. After orchidectomy the body makes little sex hormone of its own, so oestrogen is usually continued long term to protect bone.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Complications include bleeding, wound breakdown along the labia or introitus, granulation tissue, loss of depth or stenosis from insufficient dilation and, rarely, a fistula between the canal and the rectum or urethra, which presents as stool or urine in the canal. Stool or urine passing into the canal, heavy bleeding or fever needs urgent assessment by the surgical team. Urinary tract infection is a recognised complication after surgery, and the repositioned meatus can give a stream that sprays or deflects. Because the prostate is retained, benign enlargement and prostate cancer remain possible; the gland can be felt through the anterior wall, and prostate-specific antigen is interpreted knowing that oestrogen and anti-androgens lower it. There is no cervix, so cervical screening is not needed, although sexually transmitted infections can affect the canal. Breast screening follows the guidance for trans women on oestrogen. Examination needs a small speculum and lubricant, remembering that depth, axis and lining differ from those of a vagina.
