organs.name: Neophallus
organs.summary: The penis created by phalloplasty (a tube of skin and its blood vessels, usually from the forearm or thigh) or metoidioplasty (the testosterone-enlarged clitoris released to stand free), often with a lengthened urethra and a scrotum with implants.

article.title: Neophallus Anatomy
article.intro: A neophallus is a penis constructed by surgery, most often as gender-affirming surgery for trans men and some non-binary people, and also after loss of the penis through injury or cancer. Phalloplasty builds the phallus from a flap of skin, fat and fascia taken with its own vessels and nerves, usually from the forearm or thigh, while metoidioplasty releases the clitoris enlarged by testosterone to stand free as a small phallus. Neither has erectile tissue beyond that of the clitoris, so structure, sensation and function depend on the tissue used and the stages completed.

keyFacts.label: Commonest donor site
keyFacts.value: Radial forearm free flap: skin, fat and fascia on the radial artery, cephalic vein and antebrachial cutaneous nerves

keyFacts.label: Alternative
keyFacts.value: Anterolateral thigh flap on the descending branch of the lateral circumflex femoral artery, usually kept on its pedicle

keyFacts.label: Urethra
keyFacts.value: When urethral lengthening is chosen, a tube within a tube of flap skin is joined to a urethra lengthened with labia minora and vaginal mucosa

keyFacts.label: Sensation
keyFacts.value: Flap nerves joined to a dorsal clitoral nerve and the ilioinguinal nerve; returns over months to a year or more

keyFacts.label: Erection
keyFacts.value: No erectile tissue in a phalloplasty; an inflatable or malleable implant is added at a later stage

keyFacts.label: Metoidioplasty
keyFacts.value: Releases the testosterone-enlarged clitoris, typically several centimetres long, in one stage with no donor site

keyFacts.label: Retained organs
keyFacts.value: In people assigned female at birth there is no prostate; the cervix, uterus and ovaries remain unless removed and still need care

sections.heading: Location and relations
sections.body: The neophallus is attached to the pubic region where the clitoris and labia were, its base over the pubic symphysis between the hip bones and above the urethral opening. In phalloplasty the clitoris is usually stripped of its surface skin and buried at the base of the new shaft, and the labia majora are joined below to form a scrotum. If the urethra is lengthened, the new urethra runs from the original meatus through a lengthened perineal segment and along the underside of the shaft to the tip; the vagina is usually removed, because a lengthened urethra beside a retained vagina is prone to fistula. Behind lie the perineal body, external anal sphincter and rectum. The urethra passes through the urogenital hiatus of the levator ani, between the pubococcygeus of each side, and then through the deep perineal pouch, where the external urethral sphincter surrounds it, and on through the perineal membrane; the puborectalis sling lies behind, around the anorectal junction.

sections.heading: Structure
sections.body: A phalloplasty shaft is a rolled flap: an outer tube of skin over fat and deep fascia, and a glans shaped later by a ridge and skin graft (glansplasty). The radial forearm free flap is a rectangle of skin taken with the radial artery, the cephalic vein and the lateral and medial antebrachial cutaneous nerves; a narrower strip of the same flap is rolled skin-inward to form the urethra. The anterolateral thigh flap, raised on the descending branch of the lateral circumflex femoral artery, is thicker, usually stays on its pedicle and often needs a separate urethral lining. A metoidioplasty phallus is the clitoris itself, released from its suspensory ligament and the labia minora, with a urethra optionally built along its underside from labial and vaginal mucosa. Scrotoplasty from the labia majora with testicular implants completes either operation.

sections.heading: Blood supply and lymph
sections.body: A free flap lives only through its vascular pedicle. In radial forearm phalloplasty the radial artery is joined under the microscope to a recipient vessel in the groin, usually the deep inferior epigastric artery or a branch of the femoral artery, and the cephalic and accompanying veins to the great saphenous or femoral veins; the joins are watched closely for the first days, since thrombosis threatens the whole phallus. The hand keeps its supply through the ulnar artery and the palmar arches, confirmed before surgery. A pedicled anterolateral thigh flap keeps its own artery and vein from the lateral circumflex femoral system, so no microsurgery is needed. A metoidioplasty phallus keeps the clitoral branches of the internal pudendal vessels, so its erectile tissue still engorges. Lymph from the shaft skin drains to the superficial inguinal nodes.

sections.heading: Innervation
sections.body: Protective sensation comes from the flap's own cutaneous nerves, the antebrachial cutaneous nerves of the forearm or the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve of the thigh, which are joined at the base of the phallus to the ilioinguinal nerve and to one of the dorsal clitoral nerves. Erotic sensation comes from the clitoris, whose dorsal nerves are branches of the pudendal nerve (S2 to S4) and are preserved when it is buried at the base of the shaft. Regrowth is slow: the shaft is numb at first, sensation returns from base towards tip over months to a year or more, and the tip may never be as sensitive as the base. In metoidioplasty the clitoral nerves are preserved, so erotic sensation is usually retained from the outset. The forearm donor site is left with altered sensation.

sections.heading: Function and hormonal influence
sections.body: The aims are standing urination, sexual function and a body that matches the person's gender. A phalloplasty shaft has no erectile tissue, so it cannot become erect on its own; rigidity for penetration comes from an erectile device, inflatable or malleable, placed at a later stage once protective sensation has returned so the skin can guard against pressure damage. Orgasm comes from the buried clitoris and the reinnervated shaft. A metoidioplasty phallus keeps the natural erection and full sensation of clitoral tissue but is small, so penetrative sex is usually not possible; it allows standing urination if the urethra is lengthened. Testosterone maintains libido, clitoral size and the oiliness and hair of the skin; the shaft skin behaves as forearm or thigh skin, growing hair unless removed beforehand, and does not engorge with arousal.

sections.heading: Changes through the stages and over life
sections.body: Phalloplasty and metoidioplasty are options in gender-affirming care that some, not all, trans men and non-binary people choose; gender incongruence is not a mental illness, and the World Health Organization classifies it under conditions related to sexual health. A neophallus is built in stages over a year or more. Before surgery testosterone has usually enlarged the clitoris, and hair is removed from the donor skin that will line the urethra; hysterectomy and oophorectomy often precede the first stage, and vaginectomy is done when the urethra is lengthened. Later stages add glansplasty, scrotoplasty with testicular implants and, after sensation returns, an erectile implant. Swelling settles over months and the forearm scar matures over a year. The shaft is skin and fat, so unlike the clitoris it does not enlarge or shrink with hormone levels, although its skin ages and grows hair as forearm or thigh skin does, and implants have a finite life.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Urethral complications are the commonest problems after phalloplasty with urethral lengthening: a fistula, with urine leaking from the perineal or shaft urethra, and a stricture, with scar narrowing the channel and slowing the stream, which may need dilatation, urethrotomy or graft repair. Flap loss from thrombosis is rare but serious and needs an urgent return to theatre. Erectile implants can become infected or erode through the skin, since there is no corporal tissue to anchor them. The forearm donor site is covered with a skin graft that can heal slowly or fail in part, and leaves a visible scar and altered sensation; hand function is usually preserved but the arm is splinted at first. Urinary infections and retention can follow the urethral stages. Screening follows the anatomy present: a retained cervix still needs cervical screening, which has to be requested from the GP by anyone registered as male, because invitations are issued on the gender marker held by the practice; a retained uterus or ovaries still need gynaecological care, there is no prostate, and residual breast tissue after chest surgery still needs assessment if a lump appears. Anyone catheterising a neophallus should know which stages are complete, as the urethra may be tortuous.

organs.summary: The master gland at the base of the brain, controlling growth, thyroid, adrenal and reproductive hormones.

organs.name: Vertebral column

article.title: Spine Anatomy
article.intro: The vertebral column is a stack of 33 vertebrae, 24 of them movable, separated by shock-absorbing discs and bound by ligaments and muscles. It carries the weight of the head and trunk, allows the trunk to bend and twist, and shelters the spinal cord and the nerve roots that leave it at every level.

keyFacts.label: Vertebrae
keyFacts.value: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 fused sacral, 4 fused coccygeal

keyFacts.label: Curves
keyFacts.value: Cervical and lumbar lordosis, thoracic and sacral kyphosis

keyFacts.label: Discs
keyFacts.value: 23 intervertebral discs, about a quarter of the column's height

keyFacts.label: Spinal cord
keyFacts.value: Ends at about L1-L2 in adults; nerve roots continue as the cauda equina

keyFacts.label: Nerves
keyFacts.value: 31 pairs of spinal nerves leaving through the intervertebral foramina

keyFacts.label: Movement
keyFacts.value: Most flexion and extension in the cervical and lumbar spine; rotation mainly thoracic

sections.heading: A typical vertebra
sections.body: Each movable vertebra has a weight-bearing body in front and a bony arch behind that encloses the vertebral foramen; stacked, these foramina form the vertebral canal for the spinal cord. The arch carries a spinous process (the bump felt under the skin), two transverse processes and four articular facets that form small synovial joints with the vertebrae above and below. The facet joints guide movement and can wear like any other joint.

sections.heading: Regions
sections.body: The cervical vertebrae are small, with holes in their transverse processes for the vertebral arteries; the atlas (C1) supports the skull and nods on it, the axis (C2) provides the peg on which the head turns. Thoracic vertebrae have facets for the ribs and long sloping spines, so the thoracic spine is stiff. Lumbar vertebrae are massive to carry the body's weight and allow bending. The sacrum wedges between the hip bones to transmit weight to the legs, and the coccyx is the vestigial tail.

sections.heading: Intervertebral discs
sections.body: Between the bodies sit discs made of a tough ring of fibrocartilage (annulus fibrosus) around a gel-like nucleus pulposus. They absorb shock, spread load and permit small movements that add up to considerable flexibility. With age the nucleus dries and the annulus cracks; a herniated disc pushes nucleus material backwards into a nerve root, most often at L4-L5 or L5-S1, causing sciatica.

sections.heading: Ligaments and muscles
sections.body: The anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments run the length of the bodies; the ligamentum flavum joins the arches; supraspinous and interspinous ligaments link the spines. Deep muscles (erector spinae, multifidus) extend and stabilise the spine; the abdominal muscles and psoas flex it. Most back pain arises from these muscles, ligaments and facet joints rather than the discs.

sections.heading: Spinal cord and nerves
sections.body: The spinal cord runs from the medulla to about the first lumbar vertebra, wrapped in the same three meninges as the brain and bathed in cerebrospinal fluid, which is why a lumbar puncture below L2 can sample the fluid safely. Thirty-one pairs of spinal nerves leave through the intervertebral foramina; each carries motor fibres to a group of muscles and sensation from a strip of skin (a dermatome). Below the cord the roots hang as the cauda equina; compression there is a surgical emergency.

sections.heading: Blood supply
sections.body: Segmental arteries from the vertebral, intercostal and lumbar arteries supply the vertebrae and send radicular branches to the cord, which also has a single anterior and two posterior spinal arteries along its length. One large radicular artery in the lower thoracic region (the artery of Adamkiewicz) supplies most of the lower cord, and its injury during aortic surgery can cause paralysis.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Mechanical back pain, disc herniation, spinal stenosis, osteoporotic vertebral fractures and spondylolisthesis are the common spinal problems. Red flags such as leg weakness, numbness in the saddle area or loss of bladder control point to cord or cauda equina compression and need an urgent MRI. Injuries are assessed by the level of the vertebra and the spinal segment affected.

organs.name: Rib cage
organs.summary: Twelve pairs of ribs, their costal cartilages and the sternum protect the heart and lungs and move with breathing.

organs.name: Bony pelvis
organs.summary: The two hip bones with the sacrum and coccyx transfer body weight to the legs and protect pelvic organs.

organs.name: Shoulder girdle
organs.summary: Clavicle and scapula link each arm to the trunk.

organs.name: Hand skeleton
organs.summary: 27 bones per hand: 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals and 14 phalanges.

organs.name: Foot skeleton
organs.summary: 26 bones per foot: 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals and 14 phalanges.

organs.name: Knee joint
organs.summary: The largest joint in the body: femur, tibia and patella held by four ligaments and cushioned by two menisci, with the fibula alongside.

article.title: Knee Joint Anatomy
article.intro: The knee is the largest joint in the body: a hinge between the femur and tibia, with the patella gliding in front, held together by four main ligaments and cushioned by two menisci. It bears several times body weight with every step and is the joint most often injured in sport and most often replaced in later life.

keyFacts.label: Type
keyFacts.value: Modified hinge (synovial) joint: flexion, extension and a little rotation

keyFacts.label: Bones
keyFacts.value: Femoral condyles, tibial plateau, patella; the fibula lies alongside but is not part of the joint

keyFacts.label: Ligaments
keyFacts.value: Anterior and posterior cruciate, medial and lateral collateral, patellar ligament

keyFacts.label: Menisci
keyFacts.value: Medial (C-shaped) and lateral (more circular) fibrocartilage pads

keyFacts.label: Movement
keyFacts.value: About 0-140 degrees of flexion; the joint locks in full extension

keyFacts.label: Blood supply
keyFacts.value: Genicular branches of the popliteal artery

sections.heading: Bones and surfaces
sections.body: The rounded femoral condyles roll and glide on the almost flat tibial plateau, an unstable arrangement that depends entirely on ligaments and muscles for stability. The patella, a sesamoid bone in the quadriceps tendon, slides in the groove between the condyles and increases the leverage of the quadriceps. The head of the fibula articulates with the tibia below the joint line and anchors the lateral collateral ligament.

sections.heading: Ligaments
sections.body: Inside the joint the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) stops the tibia sliding forward and limits rotation; the posterior cruciate stops it sliding back. The medial collateral ligament resists the knee being forced inwards (valgus) and blends with the medial meniscus; the lateral collateral is a separate cord resisting varus force. The patellar ligament carries the quadriceps pull from the patella to the tibial tuberosity. A twisting fall tears the ACL with a pop and rapid swelling; a blow to the outside of the knee sprains the medial collateral.

sections.heading: Menisci
sections.body: Two crescents of fibrocartilage deepen the tibial surface, spread the load over the cartilage and absorb shock. Their outer third has a blood supply and can heal; the inner part does not. Tears cause pain along the joint line, catching and locking, and are seen on MRI or arthroscopy.

sections.heading: Capsule, bursae and synovium
sections.body: A fibrous capsule lined with synovial membrane surrounds the joint and produces the lubricating fluid; an effusion (water on the knee) stretches it. Several bursae reduce friction, including the prepatellar bursa in front of the kneecap (housemaid's knee when inflamed) and a bursa behind the knee that can swell into a Baker's cyst.

sections.heading: Muscles and movement
sections.body: The quadriceps extend the knee and the hamstrings flex it; the gastrocnemius, popliteus and the iliotibial tract also cross the joint. In the last degrees of extension the femur rotates medially on the tibia, screwing the joint tight so that standing needs little muscular effort; the popliteus unlocks it. Strong quadriceps and hamstrings are the best protection for the ligaments.

sections.heading: Blood and nerve supply
sections.body: The popliteal artery passes behind the knee and sends genicular branches around the joint that form an anastomosis, a safety net if the main artery is compressed. The tibial and common fibular nerves pass behind and beside the joint; the common fibular nerve winds round the fibular neck under the skin, where it is easily bruised, causing foot drop. Joint pain is carried by branches of the femoral, obturator, tibial and common fibular nerves, so hip disease can refer pain to the knee.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Osteoarthritis wears away the cartilage, most often in the medial compartment, causing pain, stiffness and bowing; X-rays show joint-space narrowing and a knee replacement resurfaces the worn ends. Ligament and meniscal injuries are diagnosed by examination and MRI. A hot swollen knee may be gout, pseudogout or infection, and a needle aspiration of the fluid tells them apart.

FJ3155.summary: T11, the eleventh of the twelve thoracic vertebrae. Thoracic vertebrae carry facets for the ribs and have long, downward-sloping spinous processes.
FJ3155.function: Bears load, protects the spinal cord and provides attachment for muscles and ligaments; an intervertebral disc separates it from its neighbours.

FJ3199.summary: A light, spongy bone between the orbits forming the roof of the nasal cavity.
FJ3199.function: Its cribriform plate is pierced by the olfactory nerves; its air cells form the ethmoidal sinuses.

FJ3169.function: Bears load, protects the spinal cord and provides attachment for muscles and ligaments; an intervertebral disc separates it from its neighbours.

FJ3157.summary: L1, the first of the five lumbar vertebrae. Lumbar vertebrae are the largest, built to carry the weight of the upper body.
FJ3157.function: Bears load, protects the spinal cord and provides attachment for muscles and ligaments; an intervertebral disc separates it from its neighbours.

FJ3200.summary: The bone of the forehead and the roof of the orbits.
FJ3200.function: Protects the frontal lobes and forms the upper margins of the eye sockets; it contains the frontal sinuses.
FJ3200.clinical: Frontal sinusitis and forehead fractures may involve the underlying brain.

FJ2772.summary: A U-shaped bone in the front of the neck, unique in articulating with no other bone.
FJ2772.function: Suspended by muscles and ligaments, it anchors the tongue and larynx during swallowing and speech.
FJ2772.clinical: A fractured hyoid is a classic sign of strangulation.

FJ3256.summary: The heel bone, the largest bone of the foot.
FJ3256.function: Forms the heel, bears weight on standing and anchors the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon.
FJ3256.clinical: Fractured in falls from height; plantar fasciitis causes pain at its underside.

FJ3257.summary: The largest carpal bone, in the centre of the wrist.
FJ3257.function: Articulates with the third metacarpal and forms the keystone of the carpal arch.

FJ3237.summary: The collarbone: an S-shaped bone running from the sternum to the acromion of the scapula.
FJ3237.function: Acts as a strut holding the shoulder away from the chest so the arm can swing freely; it is the only bony link between the arm and the trunk.
FJ3237.clinical: One of the most frequently fractured bones, usually in its middle third after a fall on the shoulder.

FJ3258.summary: The cube-shaped tarsal bone on the outer side of the midfoot.
FJ3258.function: Supports the lateral arch and provides a groove for the tendon of fibularis longus.

FJ3235.summary: The eighth rib on the left side, a false rib whose cartilage joins the cartilage above. Ribs articulate with the thoracic vertebrae behind and curve round to protect the chest organs.
FJ3235.function: Protects the heart and lungs and moves with the intercostal muscles during breathing.

FJ3226.summary: The eleventh rib on the left side, a floating rib with no anterior attachment. Ribs articulate with the thoracic vertebrae behind and curve round to protect the chest organs.
FJ3226.function: Protects the heart and lungs and moves with the intercostal muscles during breathing.

FJ3259.summary: The thigh bone: the longest and strongest bone in the body, running from the hip joint to the knee.
FJ3259.function: Carries the weight of the trunk to the leg and anchors the muscles of the hip and thigh; its head sits in the acetabulum of the hip bone and its condyles form the knee with the tibia.
FJ3259.clinical: Hip fractures through the femoral neck are common in older adults with osteoporosis; the femoral shaft breaks only with major force.

FJ3260.summary: The slender lateral bone of the lower leg, running beside the tibia to form the outer ankle (lateral malleolus).
FJ3260.function: Bears little weight but anchors leg muscles and stabilises the ankle joint.
FJ3260.clinical: The lateral malleolus is broken in many ankle fractures; the fibula is also harvested for bone grafts.

FJ3251.summary: Hyaline cartilage joining the fifth rib to the sternum on the left side, giving the rib cage elasticity.
FJ3251.function: Lets the chest wall expand and recoil with each breath.

FJ3252.summary: The fifth metacarpal on the left side: a long bone of the palm between the carpal bones and the phalanges.
FJ3252.function: Forms the framework of the hand and transmits force to the digits.

FJ3253.summary: The fifth metatarsal on the left side: a long bone of the sole between the tarsal bones and the phalanges.
FJ3253.function: Forms the framework of the foot and transmits force to the digits.

FJ3232.summary: The fifth rib on the left side, a true rib, joined to the sternum by its own costal cartilage. Ribs articulate with the thoracic vertebrae behind and curve round to protect the chest organs.
FJ3232.function: Protects the heart and lungs and moves with the intercostal muscles during breathing.

FJ3239.summary: Hyaline cartilage joining the first rib to the sternum on the left side, giving the rib cage elasticity.
FJ3239.function: Lets the chest wall expand and recoil with each breath.

FJ3240.summary: The first metacarpal on the left side: a long bone of the palm between the carpal bones and the phalanges.
FJ3240.function: Forms the framework of the hand and transmits force to the digits.

FJ3241.summary: The first metatarsal on the left side: a long bone of the sole between the tarsal bones and the phalanges.
FJ3241.function: Forms the framework of the foot and transmits force to the digits.

FJ3228.summary: The first rib on the left side, a true rib, joined to the sternum by its own costal cartilage. Ribs articulate with the thoracic vertebrae behind and curve round to protect the chest organs.

FJ3248.summary: Hyaline cartilage joining the fourth rib to the sternum on the left side, giving the rib cage elasticity.

FJ3249.function: Forms the framework of the hand and transmits force to the digits.

FJ3250.summary: The fourth metatarsal on the left side: a long bone of the sole between the tarsal bones and the phalanges.
FJ3250.function: Forms the framework of the foot and transmits force to the digits.

FJ3231.summary: The fourth rib on the left side, a true rib, joined to the sternum by its own costal cartilage. Ribs articulate with the thoracic vertebrae behind and curve round to protect the chest organs.
FJ3231.function: Protects the heart and lungs and moves with the intercostal muscles during breathing.

FJ3261.summary: The wedge-shaped carpal bone on the little-finger side with a hook projecting into the palm.
FJ3261.function: The hook forms part of the carpal tunnel and anchors the flexor retinaculum.
FJ3261.clinical: Hook of hamate fractures occur in golfers and racquet sports.

FJ3288.summary: The large, irregular bone formed by the fusion of the ilium, ischium and pubis; the two hip bones and the sacrum make up the bony pelvis.
FJ3288.function: Transfers the weight of the upper body to the legs through the hip joint (acetabulum) and protects the pelvic organs.
FJ3288.clinical: Pelvic fractures usually follow high-energy trauma; the iliac crest is a common site for bone-marrow sampling.

FJ3262.summary: The bone of the upper arm, from the shoulder to the elbow.
FJ3262.function: Its rounded head articulates with the scapula's glenoid cavity; the distal end forms the elbow with the radius and ulna. It anchors the deltoid, biceps and triceps.
FJ3262.clinical: Fractures of the surgical neck (in older adults) and shaft may injure the axillary or radial nerve.

FJ3263.summary: A scroll-shaped bone projecting into the nasal cavity from its lateral wall.
FJ3263.function: Increases the surface area that warms and humidifies inhaled air.

FJ3264.summary: The smallest cuneiform, between the medial and lateral cuneiforms.

FJ3265.summary: The smallest bone of the face, in the inner wall of the orbit.
FJ3265.function: Houses the lacrimal sac, which drains tears into the nose.

FJ3267.summary: The outer of the three cuneiform bones.
FJ3267.function: Supports the third metatarsal and contributes to the transverse arch.

FJ3268.summary: The crescent-shaped carpal bone in the centre of the proximal row.
FJ3268.function: Articulates with the radius to form the main part of the wrist joint.
FJ3268.clinical: Lunate dislocation and Kienbock's disease (avascular necrosis) affect this bone.

FJ3269.summary: The upper jaw bone, holding the upper teeth and forming much of the face.
FJ3269.function: Forms the floor of the orbit, the side of the nose and the hard palate; contains the maxillary sinus.
FJ3269.clinical: Maxillary sinusitis is the commonest sinus infection; Le Fort fractures separate the maxilla from the skull.

FJ3271.summary: The largest of the three wedge-shaped bones in front of the navicular.
FJ3271.function: Articulates with the first metatarsal and supports the medial arch.

FJ3272.summary: One of two small bones forming the bridge of the nose.
FJ3272.function: Supports the upper part of the nose.
FJ3272.clinical: The most frequently fractured facial bone.

FJ3236.summary: The ninth rib on the left side, a false rib whose cartilage joins the cartilage above. Ribs articulate with the thoracic vertebrae behind and curve round to protect the chest organs.
FJ3236.function: Protects the heart and lungs and moves with the intercostal muscles during breathing.

FJ3273.summary: An L-shaped bone forming the back of the hard palate and part of the nasal cavity and orbit.
FJ3273.function: Separates the mouth from the nasal cavity.

FJ3274.function: Protects the parietal lobes of the brain.
FJ3274.clinical: Skull fractures here can tear the middle meningeal artery and cause an extradural haematoma.

FJ3275.summary: The kneecap: a triangular sesamoid bone embedded in the quadriceps tendon in front of the knee.
FJ3275.function: Increases the leverage of the quadriceps and protects the front of the knee joint.
FJ3275.clinical: Patellar dislocation and patellofemoral pain are common in young, active people.

FJ3276.summary: A pea-sized sesamoid bone in the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris.
FJ3276.function: Increases the leverage of flexor carpi ulnaris and forms a wall of the ulnar canal.

FJ3277.summary: The lateral bone of the forearm, on the thumb side, wider at the wrist than at the elbow.
FJ3277.function: Rotates around the ulna to turn the palm up and down (supination and pronation) and carries most of the load across the wrist joint.
FJ3277.clinical: A fall on the outstretched hand often breaks the distal radius (Colles fracture).

FJ3278.summary: The boat-shaped carpal bone on the thumb side of the wrist.
FJ3278.function: Links the two rows of carpal bones and bears load across the wrist.
FJ3278.clinical: The most commonly fractured carpal bone; its poor blood supply makes non-union and avascular necrosis a risk.

FJ3279.summary: The shoulder blade: a flat triangular bone lying against the back of the rib cage.
FJ3279.function: Its glenoid cavity forms the shoulder joint with the humerus; its spine and acromion anchor the deltoid and trapezius, and it glides over the ribs to widen the reach of the arm.
FJ3279.clinical: Scapular fractures are rare and signal severe chest trauma.

FJ3242.summary: Hyaline cartilage joining the second rib to the sternum on the left side, giving the rib cage elasticity.
FJ3242.function: Lets the chest wall expand and recoil with each breath.

FJ3243.summary: The second metacarpal on the left side: a long bone of the palm between the carpal bones and the phalanges.
FJ3243.function: Forms the framework of the hand and transmits force to the digits.

FJ3244.summary: The second metatarsal on the left side: a long bone of the sole between the tarsal bones and the phalanges.
FJ3244.function: Forms the framework of the foot and transmits force to the digits.

FJ3229.summary: The second rib on the left side, a true rib, joined to the sternum by its own costal cartilage. Ribs articulate with the thoracic vertebrae behind and curve round to protect the chest organs.
FJ3229.function: Protects the heart and lungs and moves with the intercostal muscles during breathing.

FJ3255.summary: Hyaline cartilage joining the seventh rib to the sternum on the left side, giving the rib cage elasticity.
FJ3255.function: Lets the chest wall expand and recoil with each breath.

FJ3280.summary: The ankle bone, sitting on the calcaneus and gripped between the tibia and fibula.
FJ3280.function: Transmits the whole weight of the body from the leg to the foot; it has no muscle attachments.
FJ3280.clinical: Talar fractures risk avascular necrosis because of the bone's limited blood supply.

FJ3281.summary: A complex bone at the side and base of the skull housing the ear.
FJ3281.function: Contains the middle and inner ear, forms the jaw joint with the mandible and gives attachment to neck muscles through the mastoid process.
FJ3281.clinical: Temporal bone fractures may cause hearing loss or facial nerve palsy.

FJ3282.summary: The shin bone: the larger, weight-bearing bone of the lower leg, from the knee to the ankle.
FJ3282.function: Transmits body weight from the femur to the talus; its sharp anterior border lies just under the skin of the shin.
FJ3282.clinical: Tibial shaft fractures are the commonest long-bone fractures; stress fractures affect runners.

FJ3283.summary: The carpal bone at the base of the thumb.
FJ3283.function: Its saddle-shaped joint with the first metacarpal gives the thumb its wide range of movement.
FJ3283.clinical: Osteoarthritis of the trapeziometacarpal joint causes pain at the base of the thumb.

FJ3284.summary: A small wedge-shaped carpal bone at the base of the index finger.

FJ3285.summary: The three-cornered carpal bone on the little-finger side of the proximal row.
FJ3285.function: Articulates with the pisiform and helps transmit force from the hand to the ulna side.

FJ3227.summary: The twelfth rib on the left side, a floating rib with no anterior attachment. Ribs articulate with the thoracic vertebrae behind and curve round to protect the chest organs.
FJ3227.function: Protects the heart and lungs and moves with the intercostal muscles during breathing.

FJ3286.summary: The medial bone of the forearm, on the little-finger side, with the olecranon forming the point of the elbow.
FJ3286.function: Forms the hinge of the elbow with the humerus and the pivot around which the radius rotates.
FJ3286.clinical: The olecranon can be fractured by a direct blow to the elbow.

FJ3287.summary: The cheekbone, forming the prominence of the cheek and the outer wall of the orbit.
FJ3287.function: Protects the eye and gives origin to the masseter muscle.
FJ3287.clinical: Zygomatic fractures flatten the cheek and may trap eye muscles.

FJ3289.summary: The lower jaw, the largest and strongest bone of the face and the only movable skull bone.
FJ3289.function: Holds the lower teeth and articulates with the temporal bones at the jaw joints; the muscles of mastication move it.
FJ3289.clinical: Mandibular fractures are common in assaults; the temporomandibular joint is a frequent source of facial pain.

FJ3290.summary: The upper, wider part of the sternum, joined to the clavicles and the first ribs.
FJ3290.function: Forms the sternoclavicular joints; the notch at its top can be felt at the base of the neck.
FJ3290.clinical: The junction with the body of the sternum (sternal angle) is a landmark for counting ribs.

FJ3307.function: Forms the highest point of the medial arch of the foot.
FJ3307.clinical: Navicular stress fractures occur in athletes.

FJ3175.function: Bears load, protects the spinal cord and provides attachment for muscles and ligaments; an intervertebral disc separates it from its neighbours.

FJ3309.summary: The bone at the back and base of the skull, pierced by the foramen magnum.
FJ3309.function: Protects the occipital lobes and cerebellum; the spinal cord passes through the foramen magnum, and the occipital condyles rest on the atlas.
FJ3309.clinical: Fractures of the skull base can leak cerebrospinal fluid from the ear or nose.

FJ3360.summary: The heel bone, the largest bone of the foot.
FJ3360.function: Forms the heel, bears weight on standing and anchors the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon.
FJ3360.clinical: Fractured in falls from height; plantar fasciitis causes pain at its underside.

FJ3361.summary: The largest carpal bone, in the centre of the wrist.
FJ3361.function: Articulates with the third metacarpal and forms the keystone of the carpal arch.

FJ3362.summary: The collarbone: an S-shaped bone running from the sternum to the acromion of the scapula.
FJ3362.function: Acts as a strut holding the shoulder away from the chest so the arm can swing freely; it is the only bony link between the arm and the trunk.
FJ3362.clinical: One of the most frequently fractured bones, usually in its middle third after a fall on the shoulder.

FJ3364.summary: The cube-shaped tarsal bone on the outer side of the midfoot.
FJ3364.function: Supports the lateral arch and provides a groove for the tendon of fibularis longus.

FJ3347.summary: The eighth rib on the right side, a false rib whose cartilage joins the cartilage above. Ribs articulate with the thoracic vertebrae behind and curve round to protect the chest organs.
FJ3347.function: Protects the heart and lungs and moves with the intercostal muscles during breathing.

FJ3331.summary: The eleventh rib on the right side, a floating rib with no anterior attachment. Ribs articulate with the thoracic vertebrae behind and curve round to protect the chest organs.
FJ3331.function: Protects the heart and lungs and moves with the intercostal muscles during breathing.

FJ3365.summary: The thigh bone: the longest and strongest bone in the body, running from the hip joint to the knee.
FJ3365.function: Carries the weight of the trunk to the leg and anchors the muscles of the hip and thigh; its head sits in the acetabulum of the hip bone and its condyles form the knee with the tibia.
FJ3365.clinical: Hip fractures through the femoral neck are common in older adults with osteoporosis; the femoral shaft breaks only with major force.

FJ3366.summary: The slender lateral bone of the lower leg, running beside the tibia to form the outer ankle (lateral malleolus).
FJ3366.function: Bears little weight but anchors leg muscles and stabilises the ankle joint.
FJ3366.clinical: The lateral malleolus is broken in many ankle fractures; the fibula is also harvested for bone grafts.

FJ3340.function: Protects the heart and lungs and moves with the intercostal muscles during breathing.

FJ3367.summary: The wedge-shaped carpal bone on the little-finger side with a hook projecting into the palm.
FJ3367.function: The hook forms part of the carpal tunnel and anchors the flexor retinaculum.
FJ3367.clinical: Hook of hamate fractures occur in golfers and racquet sports.

FJ3152.summary: The large, irregular bone formed by the fusion of the ilium, ischium and pubis; the two hip bones and the sacrum make up the bony pelvis.
FJ3152.function: Transfers the weight of the upper body to the legs through the hip joint (acetabulum) and protects the pelvic organs.
FJ3152.clinical: Pelvic fractures usually follow high-energy trauma; the iliac crest is a common site for bone-marrow sampling.

FJ3368.summary: The bone of the upper arm, from the shoulder to the elbow.
FJ3368.function: Its rounded head articulates with the scapula's glenoid cavity; the distal end forms the elbow with the radius and ulna. It anchors the deltoid, biceps and triceps.
FJ3368.clinical: Fractures of the surgical neck (in older adults) and shaft may injure the axillary or radial nerve.

FJ3369.summary: A scroll-shaped bone projecting into the nasal cavity from its lateral wall.
FJ3369.function: Increases the surface area that warms and humidifies inhaled air.

FJ3370.summary: The smallest cuneiform, between the medial and lateral cuneiforms.

FJ3371.summary: The smallest bone of the face, in the inner wall of the orbit.
FJ3371.function: Houses the lacrimal sac, which drains tears into the nose.

FJ3373.summary: The outer of the three cuneiform bones.
FJ3373.function: Supports the third metatarsal and contributes to the transverse arch.

FJ3374.summary: The crescent-shaped carpal bone in the centre of the proximal row.
FJ3374.function: Articulates with the radius to form the main part of the wrist joint.
FJ3374.clinical: Lunate dislocation and Kienbock's disease (avascular necrosis) affect this bone.

FJ3375.summary: The upper jaw bone, holding the upper teeth and forming much of the face.
FJ3375.function: Forms the floor of the orbit, the side of the nose and the hard palate; contains the maxillary sinus.
FJ3375.clinical: Maxillary sinusitis is the commonest sinus infection; Le Fort fractures separate the maxilla from the skull.

FJ3377.summary: The largest of the three wedge-shaped bones in front of the navicular.
FJ3377.function: Articulates with the first metatarsal and supports the medial arch.

FJ3378.summary: One of two small bones forming the bridge of the nose.
FJ3378.function: Supports the upper part of the nose.
FJ3378.clinical: The most frequently fractured facial bone.

FJ3348.summary: The ninth rib on the right side, a false rib whose cartilage joins the cartilage above. Ribs articulate with the thoracic vertebrae behind and curve round to protect the chest organs.
FJ3348.function: Protects the heart and lungs and moves with the intercostal muscles during breathing.

FJ3379.summary: An L-shaped bone forming the back of the hard palate and part of the nasal cavity and orbit.
FJ3379.function: Separates the mouth from the nasal cavity.

FJ3380.summary: One of a pair of large curved bones forming the sides and roof of the skull.
FJ3380.function: Protects the parietal lobes of the brain.
FJ3380.clinical: Skull fractures here can tear the middle meningeal artery and cause an extradural haematoma.

FJ1477M.function: The main extensor of the elbow, essential for pushing and throwing.
FJ1477M.clinical: Supplied by the radial nerve; weakness of extension follows radial nerve injury.

FJ1393.summary: Lateral head of right flexor hallucis brevis is part of the flexor hallucis brevis. A short muscle in the sole with two heads inserting on the big toe.
FJ1393.function: Flexes the big toe at its base.

FJ1394.summary: Lateral head of right gastrocnemius is part of the gastrocnemius. The two-headed calf muscle forming the bulge of the calf, from the femoral condyles to the Achilles tendon.
FJ1394.function: Plantar flexes the ankle (rising on the toes) and helps flex the knee; the power muscle of walking, running and jumping.
FJ1394.clinical: 'Tennis leg' is a tear of the medial head; calf strains are common in sport.

FJ1477.summary: Lateral head of right triceps brachii is part of the triceps brachii. The three-headed muscle on the back of the upper arm, inserting on the olecranon of the ulna.
FJ1477.function: The main extensor of the elbow, essential for pushing and throwing.
FJ1477.clinical: Supplied by the radial nerve; weakness of extension follows radial nerve injury.

FJ1547M.summary: Small muscles between the lumbar transverse processes.
FJ1547M.function: Bend the spine sideways and stabilise it.

FJ1547.summary: Small muscles between the lumbar transverse processes.
FJ1547.function: Bend the spine sideways and stabilise it.

FJ1400M.summary: A muscle along the inner border of the sole.
FJ1400M.function: Abducts and flexes the big toe and supports the medial arch.

FJ1483M.summary: The superficial muscle of the thenar eminence at the base of the thumb.
FJ1483M.function: Moves the thumb away from the palm.
FJ1483M.clinical: Wastes in carpal tunnel syndrome because it is supplied by the median nerve.

FJ1484M.summary: A deep forearm muscle whose tendon reaches the first metacarpal.
FJ1484M.function: Abducts and extends the thumb at its base.

FJ1401M.summary: A short adductor muscle beneath adductor longus.
FJ1401M.function: Adducts the thigh and assists hip flexion.

FJ1402M.summary: The most superficial adductor, from the pubis to the middle of the femur.
FJ1402M.function: Adducts the thigh, bringing the legs together.
FJ1402M.clinical: The usual site of 'groin strain' in football and hockey.

FJ1403M.summary: The largest adductor, a broad triangular sheet on the inner thigh with an adductor and a hamstring part.
FJ1403M.function: Adducts the thigh; its hamstring part extends the hip.
FJ1403M.clinical: The femoral artery passes through its adductor hiatus to reach the back of the knee.

FJ1404M.summary: The upper, partly separate portion of adductor magnus.
FJ1404M.function: Adducts and laterally rotates the thigh.

FJ1485M.summary: A small triangular muscle at the back of the elbow.
FJ1485M.function: Assists triceps in extending the elbow and stabilises the joint.

FJ2774.summary: A muscle in the aryepiglottic fold.
FJ2774.function: Helps close the inlet of the larynx during swallowing.

FJ1486M.summary: A broad muscle lying under the biceps, from the humerus to the ulna.
FJ1486M.function: The strongest flexor of the elbow, working in every position of the forearm.

FJ1487M.summary: The muscle forming the bulk of the lateral forearm, from the humerus to the distal radius.
FJ1487M.function: Flexes the elbow, most effectively with the forearm midway between pronation and supination.

FJ1405M.summary: The Achilles tendon: the thickest and strongest tendon in the body, from the calf muscles to the heel.
FJ1405M.function: Transmits the pull of gastrocnemius and soleus to the calcaneus to lift the heel.
FJ1405M.clinical: Rupture feels like a kick to the back of the ankle; tendinopathy affects runners.

FJ1524M.summary: Deep rotator muscles of the cervical spine.

FJ1449M.summary: A muscle behind the levator ani from the ischial spine to the coccyx.
FJ1449M.function: Supports the pelvic floor and flexes the coccyx.

FJ1291.summary: The fibrous ring at the apex of the orbit from which the four rectus muscles arise.
FJ1291.function: Anchors the rectus muscles; the optic nerve and the nerves to the eye muscles pass through it.

FJ1488M.summary: A small muscle from the coracoid process to the middle of the humerus.
FJ1488M.function: Flexes and adducts the arm at the shoulder.

FJ1555.summary: A muscle with two bellies joined by a tendon slung from the hyoid bone.
FJ1555.function: Opens the mouth by lowering the mandible and raises the hyoid in swallowing.

FJ1489M.summary: A muscle on the back of the forearm to the third metacarpal.
FJ1489M.clinical: Its origin at the lateral epicondyle is the site of tennis elbow.

FJ1490M.summary: A muscle on the back of the forearm to the second metacarpal.
FJ1490M.function: Extends and abducts the wrist, as in making a fist.

FJ1472M.summary: A muscle along the ulnar side of the back of the forearm to the fifth metacarpal.

FJ1491M.summary: A slender muscle with a tendon to the little finger.

FJ1492M.summary: The main extensor of the fingers, whose tendons fan across the back of the hand.

FJ1406M.summary: A muscle on the front of the leg whose tendons reach the four lesser toes.
FJ1406M.function: Extends the toes and dorsiflexes the foot.

FJ1407M.summary: A small muscle on the top of the foot reaching the big toe.

FJ1408M.summary: A deep muscle of the front of the leg with a tendon to the big toe.
FJ1408M.function: Extends the big toe and dorsiflexes the ankle.
FJ1408M.clinical: Its strength tests the L5 nerve root.

FJ1493M.summary: A deep forearm muscle with a tendon to the index finger.
FJ1493M.function: Extends the index finger independently, as in pointing.

FJ1494M.summary: A small muscle with a tendon to the base of the thumb.
FJ1494M.function: Extends the thumb at its middle joint.
FJ1494M.clinical: Inflamed with abductor pollicis longus in De Quervain's tenosynovitis.

FJ1495M.summary: A deep forearm muscle whose tendon forms the ulnar border of the anatomical snuffbox.
FJ1495M.function: Extends the thumb tip and lifts the thumb away from the palm.

FJ1452M.summary: The largest and most superficial of the flat abdominal muscles, with fibres running like hands in pockets.
FJ1452M.function: Compresses the abdomen, flexes and rotates the trunk, and helps forced expiration.
FJ1452M.clinical: Its aponeurosis forms the inguinal ligament and the outer ring of the inguinal canal.

FJ1409M.summary: A muscle of the outer leg inserting on the base of the fifth metatarsal.
FJ1409M.function: Everts the foot and steadies the ankle.
FJ1409M.clinical: Violent inversion can avulse the fifth metatarsal base at its attachment.

FJ1410M.summary: A muscle on the outer side of the leg whose tendon crosses under the sole to the first metatarsal.
FJ1410M.function: Everts and plantar flexes the foot and supports the arches.
FJ1410M.clinical: Its nerve, the superficial fibular nerve, is injured by ankle sprains.

FJ1411M.summary: A small muscle beside extensor digitorum longus reaching the fifth metatarsal.

FJ1412M.summary: Quadratus plantae: a muscle of the sole attached to the tendon of flexor digitorum longus.
FJ1412M.function: Straightens the pull of flexor digitorum longus on the toes.

FJ1496M.summary: A forearm muscle from the medial epicondyle to the base of the second and third metacarpals.
FJ1496M.clinical: The radial pulse is felt just lateral to its tendon.

FJ1413M.summary: A muscle in the middle of the sole with tendons to the four lesser toes.
FJ1413M.function: Flexes the toes at their middle joints.

FJ1414M.summary: A deep calf muscle whose tendons cross the sole to the four lesser toes.
FJ1414M.function: Flexes the toes and helps plantar flex the foot.

FJ1497M.summary: A deep forearm muscle whose tendons pass through those of the superficialis to reach the fingertips.
FJ1497M.function: Flexes the fingertips; the only muscle that can flex the distal joints.

FJ1475M.summary: A large forearm muscle whose four tendons split to insert on the middle phalanges.
FJ1475M.function: Flexes the middle joints of the fingers and the wrist.

FJ1415M.summary: A deep calf muscle from the fibula with a tendon to the big toe.
FJ1415M.function: Flexes the big toe, giving the final push-off in walking.

FJ1469.summary: A thenar muscle with a superficial and a deep head.
FJ1469.function: Flexes the thumb at its base.

FJ1498M.summary: A deep forearm muscle from the radius to the tip of the thumb.
FJ1498M.function: Flexes the thumb tip, as in pinching.

FJ1416M.summary: A small muscle below the obturator internus tendon.

FJ1417M.summary: A small muscle running with the obturator internus tendon.

FJ2738.summary: The large fan-shaped muscle forming the bulk of the tongue, from the inside of the chin.
FJ2738.function: Protrudes the tongue and pulls it forward, keeping the airway open in sleep.
FJ2738.clinical: Hypoglossal nerve palsy makes the tongue deviate toward the weak side.

FJ1559.summary: A narrow muscle from the chin to the hyoid bone.
FJ1559.function: Pulls the hyoid forward and up during swallowing.

FJ1418M.summary: The largest and most superficial muscle of the buttock.
FJ1418M.function: The main extensor of the hip, used in climbing stairs, rising from a chair and running.
FJ1418M.clinical: Site of intramuscular injections in the upper outer quadrant, away from the sciatic nerve.

FJ1419M.summary: A fan-shaped muscle on the outer side of the hip, partly under gluteus maximus.
FJ1419M.function: Abducts the hip and keeps the pelvis level when standing on one leg.
FJ1419M.clinical: Weakness produces a Trendelenburg gait, with the pelvis dropping on the opposite side.

FJ1420M.summary: The smallest and deepest of the gluteal muscles.
FJ1420M.function: Abducts and medially rotates the hip and steadies the pelvis in walking.

FJ1421M.summary: A long, thin muscle on the inner thigh from the pubis to the tibia.
FJ1421M.function: Adducts the thigh and flexes the knee.
FJ1421M.clinical: Often harvested for tendon and muscle grafts.

FJ2739.summary: A thin muscle from the hyoid bone into the side of the tongue.

FJ1422M.summary: A fan-shaped muscle filling the inside of the ilium.
FJ1422M.function: Joins psoas major (as iliopsoas) to flex the hip.

FJ1453M.summary: The lateral part of the levator ani, from the tendinous arch to the coccyx.

FJ1526M.summary: The upper part of the iliocostalis, from the upper ribs to the cervical vertebrae.

FJ1527M.summary: The lateral column of the erector spinae in the lumbar region, reaching the lower ribs.
FJ1527M.function: Extends and bends the lumbar spine.

FJ1528M.summary: The middle part of the iliocostalis, running between the ribs.
FJ1528M.function: Extends the thoracic spine and steadies the ribs.

FJ1423M.summary: A thick band of fascia running down the outer thigh from the hip to the tibia.
FJ1423M.function: Stabilises the knee in standing and walking.
FJ1423M.clinical: Iliotibial band syndrome causes lateral knee pain in runners and cyclists.

FJ1294.summary: The only extraocular muscle arising from the front of the orbit.
FJ1294.function: Turns the eye up and out and rotates it outward.

FJ2740.summary: The lowest and thickest pharyngeal constrictor, from the larynx.
FJ2740.function: Completes the swallow and its lower fibres act as the upper oesophageal sphincter.

FJ1295.summary: An extraocular muscle beneath the eyeball.
FJ1295.clinical: Can be trapped in fractures of the orbital floor, limiting upward gaze.

FJ1500M.summary: A rotator cuff muscle below the spine of the scapula.
FJ1500M.function: Laterally rotates the arm and stabilises the shoulder.

FJ1551M.summary: Short muscles between adjacent spinous processes.
FJ1551M.function: Extend the spine and stabilise the vertebrae.

FJ2778.summary: A small laryngeal muscle from the cricoid arch to the arytenoid.
FJ2778.function: Closes the vocal folds for phonation.

FJ1304.summary: The extraocular muscle on the outer side of the eyeball, supplied by the abducens nerve.
FJ1304.clinical: Abducens palsy causes double vision on looking to that side.

FJ1306.summary: The muscle that raises the upper eyelid.
FJ1306.function: Opens the eye; its smooth-muscle part keeps the lid up in the alert state.
FJ1306.clinical: Weakness causes drooping of the eyelid (ptosis).

FJ1532M.summary: A strap muscle from the upper cervical vertebrae to the top corner of the scapula.
FJ1532M.function: Elevates the scapula, as in shrugging.
FJ1532M.clinical: A common site of tension in neck pain.

FJ2741.summary: A muscle from the skull base into the soft palate.
FJ2741.function: Lifts the soft palate to close the nose off during swallowing and speech.

FJ1533M.summary: The part of the erector spinae reaching the mastoid process.

FJ1534M.summary: The part of the erector spinae inserting on the cervical vertebrae.

FJ1535M.summary: The largest column of the erector spinae, along the thoracic and lumbar spine.
FJ1535M.function: Extends the spine and keeps the trunk upright.

FJ1561.summary: A deep muscle on the front of the cervical spine reaching the skull base.

FJ1522M.summary: Deep rotator muscles of the lumbar spine.
FJ1522M.function: Rotate and stabilise the lumbar vertebrae.

FJ1308.summary: The extraocular muscle on the inner side of the eyeball.
FJ1308.function: Turns the eye inward toward the nose; both together converge the eyes for near vision.

FJ2754.summary: The middle constrictor of the pharynx, from the hyoid bone.

FJ1562.summary: The muscular floor of the mouth, stretched between the two sides of the mandible.
FJ1562.function: Raises the floor of the mouth and the tongue in swallowing.

FJ2780.summary: A muscle crossing from one arytenoid to the other.
FJ2780.function: Closes the laryngeal inlet during swallowing.

FJ1563.summary: A suboccipital muscle from the axis to the atlas.
FJ1563.function: Rotates the atlas, turning the head.

FJ1564.summary: A suboccipital muscle from the atlas to the occipital bone.
FJ1564.function: Extends the head and bends it sideways.

FJ1425M.summary: A flat muscle on the outer surface of the obturator membrane.

FJ1426M.summary: A muscle lining the inside of the pelvis that turns sharply to reach the femur.
FJ1426M.function: Laterally rotates the hip and steadies the femoral head.

FJ1565.summary: A two-bellied strap muscle running from the scapula across the neck to the hyoid.
FJ1565.function: Depresses the hyoid and tenses the deep cervical fascia.

FJ1501M.summary: A deep thenar muscle inserting along the first metacarpal.
FJ1501M.function: Rotates the thumb to touch the fingertips (opposition), the key to a precision grip.

FJ2743.summary: A muscle from the soft palate down into the pharynx.
FJ2743.function: Pulls the pharynx up and narrows the throat in swallowing.

FJ1502M.summary: A slender forearm muscle inserting into the palmar aponeurosis, absent in about one person in seven.
FJ1502M.function: Weakly flexes the wrist and tenses the palm.
FJ1502M.clinical: Its tendon is a favourite graft for hand surgery.

FJ1427M.summary: A flat muscle at the top of the inner thigh, from the pubis to the femur.

FJ1456M.summary: A thin triangular muscle beneath pectoralis major, from ribs 3 to 5 to the coracoid process.
FJ1456M.function: Pulls the scapula forward and down and helps lift the ribs in forced breathing.

FJ1428M.summary: A pear-shaped muscle from the sacrum to the greater trochanter, leaving the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen.
FJ1428M.function: Laterally rotates and abducts the hip.
FJ1428M.clinical: The sciatic nerve passes beneath (occasionally through) it; piriformis syndrome mimics sciatica.

FJ1429M.summary: A small muscle with a very long thin tendon running beside the Achilles tendon.
FJ1429M.function: A weak plantar flexor; its tendon is sometimes used as a graft.

FJ1558.summary: A broad, thin sheet of muscle in the superficial tissue of the neck.
FJ1558.function: Tenses the skin of the neck and draws down the corners of the mouth.

FJ1430M.summary: A small muscle at the back of the knee.
FJ1430M.function: 'Unlocks' the extended knee by rotating the femur laterally on the tibia at the start of flexion.

FJ2782.summary: A muscle on the back of the cricoid cartilage.
FJ2782.function: The only muscle that opens the vocal folds; essential for breathing.
FJ2782.clinical: Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury paralyses it and obstructs the airway.

FJ1503M.summary: A square muscle across the front of the distal forearm.
FJ1503M.function: The main pronator of the forearm.

FJ1431M.summary: A long muscle from the lumbar spine that joins the iliacus to insert on the femur.
FJ1431M.function: The most powerful flexor of the hip; also flexes the lumbar spine.
FJ1431M.clinical: A psoas abscess can track down from the spine; hip flexor tightness is common in sedentary people.

FJ2744.summary: A fibrous band between the buccinator and the superior pharyngeal constrictor.
FJ2744.function: Shared attachment for the cheek and pharynx muscles.

FJ1457M.summary: The main part of the levator ani, from the pubis to the coccyx.
FJ1457M.function: Supports the pelvic organs and helps continence.

FJ1458M.summary: A U-shaped sling of the levator ani looping behind the anorectal junction.
FJ1458M.function: Kinks the rectum forward to maintain continence and relaxes during defecation.

FJ1432M.summary: A flat, square muscle from the ischium to the femur.

FJ1566.summary: A small muscle from the atlas to the skull base.
FJ1566.function: Flexes the head at the atlanto-occipital joint.

FJ1569.summary: A small muscle from the atlas to the jugular process of the occipital bone.

FJ1567.summary: A suboccipital muscle from the spine of the axis to the occipital bone.

FJ1568.summary: A small suboccipital muscle from the atlas to the occipital bone.

FJ1433M.summary: The straight head of the quadriceps, running down the front of the thigh from the hip bone to the patella.
FJ1433M.function: Extends the knee and, uniquely among the quadriceps, also flexes the hip; used in kicking.
FJ1433M.clinical: Prone to strains in sprinters and footballers.

FJ1536M.summary: A flat muscle between the thoracic spine and the medial border of the scapula.
FJ1536M.function: Retracts the scapula, squaring the shoulders.

FJ1537M.summary: A small muscle above rhomboid major, from C7 and T1 to the scapula.

FJ2745.summary: A slender muscle from the auditory tube into the pharynx.
FJ2745.function: Raises the pharynx and helps open the auditory tube.

FJ1434M.summary: The longest muscle in the body, winding from the front of the hip bone across the thigh to the inner knee.
FJ1434M.function: Flexes, abducts and laterally rotates the hip and flexes the knee, the movement of crossing the legs.

FJ1570.summary: A neck muscle from the cervical vertebrae to the first rib.
FJ1570.function: Lifts the first rib in breathing and bends the neck sideways.
FJ1570.clinical: The brachial plexus and subclavian artery pass between the anterior and middle scalenes; tightness can cause thoracic outlet syndrome.

FJ1571.summary: The largest of the scalene muscles, from the cervical vertebrae to the first rib.
FJ1571.function: Elevates the first rib and flexes the neck laterally.

FJ1572.summary: The smallest scalene muscle, reaching the second rib.
FJ1572.function: Elevates the second rib and bends the neck sideways.

FJ1435M.summary: The deepest medial hamstring, with a broad flat tendon of origin.
FJ1435M.function: Flexes the knee, extends the hip and medially rotates the flexed leg.

FJ1538M.summary: A thick muscle of the back of the neck from the upper spine to the occipital bone.
FJ1538M.function: Extends the head and neck; a common source of tension headache.

FJ1539M.summary: A deep muscle from the upper thoracic to the cervical vertebrae.
FJ1539M.function: Extends and rotates the cervical spine.

FJ1540M.summary: A deep back muscle spanning the thoracic vertebrae.
FJ1540M.function: Extends and rotates the thoracic spine.

FJ1436M.summary: A medial hamstring with a long cord-like tendon reaching the tibia.
FJ1436M.function: Flexes the knee and extends the hip.
FJ1436M.clinical: Its tendon is commonly used to reconstruct the anterior cruciate ligament.

FJ1459M.summary: A muscle wrapping around the side of the chest from the upper ribs to the scapula.
FJ1459M.function: Pulls the scapula forward and rotates it upward, essential for punching and lifting the arm above the head.
FJ1459M.clinical: Long thoracic nerve injury causes a 'winged' scapula.

FJ1541M.summary: A thin muscle of the lower back from the spine to the lower ribs.
FJ1541M.function: Pulls the lower ribs down and out.

FJ1542M.summary: A thin muscle of the upper back from the spine to the upper ribs.
FJ1542M.function: Elevates the upper ribs in inspiration.

FJ1437M.summary: A broad flat muscle beneath gastrocnemius, from the tibia and fibula.
FJ1437M.function: Plantar flexes the ankle and keeps the body from toppling forward when standing; its pumping action returns venous blood from the leg.

FJ1544M.summary: The medial column of the erector spinae, closest to the spinous processes.

FJ1545M.summary: A broad strap muscle from the spine to the skull base, lying under trapezius.
FJ1545M.function: Extends and rotates the head; together, both sides pull the head back.

FJ1546M.summary: The lower part of the splenius, from the upper thoracic spines to the cervical transverse processes.

FJ1573.summary: The prominent strap muscle on each side of the neck, from the sternum and clavicle to the mastoid process.
FJ1573.function: Turns the head to the opposite side and tilts it to the same side; both together flex the neck.
FJ1573.clinical: Torticollis (wry neck) results from spasm or shortening of this muscle.

FJ1574.summary: A strap muscle in the front of the neck from the sternum to the hyoid.

FJ1575.summary: A strap muscle from the sternum to the thyroid cartilage.

FJ1576.summary: A slender muscle from the styloid process to the hyoid bone.
FJ1576.function: Pulls the hyoid up and back.

FJ2746.summary: A long muscle from the styloid process into the pharynx, supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve.
FJ2746.function: Elevates the pharynx and larynx during swallowing.

FJ1460M.summary: A small muscle under the clavicle, from the first rib.
FJ1460M.function: Steadies the clavicle during shoulder movements.

FJ1504M.summary: The rotator cuff muscle filling the front surface of the scapula.
FJ1504M.function: Medially rotates the arm and prevents the humeral head sliding forward.

FJ1322.summary: An extraocular muscle whose tendon passes through a fibrous pulley (trochlea) before reaching the eyeball, supplied by the trochlear nerve.
FJ1322.function: Turns the eye down and out and rotates it inward.

FJ2747.summary: The uppermost of the three overlapping muscles of the pharyngeal wall.
FJ2747.function: Squeezes the top of the pharynx to push the food bolus downward.

FJ1323.summary: An extraocular muscle on top of the eyeball, supplied by the oculomotor nerve.

FJ1505M.summary: A muscle wrapping around the upper radius.
FJ1505M.function: Supinates the forearm, especially when the elbow is straight.
FJ1505M.clinical: The deep branch of the radial nerve passes through it.

FJ1506M.summary: A rotator cuff muscle running above the spine of the scapula to the top of the humerus.
FJ1506M.function: Starts abduction of the arm and holds the humeral head in the glenoid.
FJ1506M.clinical: The most commonly torn rotator cuff tendon; impingement under the acromion causes painful arc.

FJ1438M.summary: A short muscle at the front of the hip inserting into the iliotibial tract.
FJ1438M.function: Tenses the iliotibial tract, helping to abduct and flex the hip and steady the knee.

FJ2748.summary: A muscle whose tendon hooks around the pterygoid hamulus into the soft palate.
FJ2748.function: Tenses the soft palate and opens the auditory tube (the 'pop' when swallowing).

FJ1507M.summary: A thick muscle from the lower scapula to the front of the humerus.
FJ1507M.function: Adducts, extends and medially rotates the arm, working with latissimus dorsi.

FJ1508M.summary: A small rotator cuff muscle along the lateral border of the scapula.
FJ1508M.function: Laterally rotates the arm with infraspinatus.

FJ2784.summary: A muscle inside the vocal fold from the thyroid cartilage to the arytenoid.
FJ2784.function: Relaxes and shortens the vocal ligament, lowering the pitch.

FJ1577.summary: A short muscle from the thyroid cartilage to the hyoid.
FJ1577.function: Raises the larynx or depresses the hyoid.

FJ1439M.summary: The muscle beside the shin bone on the front of the leg.
FJ1439M.function: Dorsiflexes and inverts the foot, lifting the toes in walking.
FJ1439M.clinical: Weakness (foot drop) follows common fibular nerve injury; shin splints affect its attachment.

FJ1440M.summary: The deepest muscle of the calf, its tendon passing behind the inner ankle.
FJ1440M.function: Inverts and plantar flexes the foot and supports the medial arch.
FJ1440M.clinical: Tendon failure leads to a progressive flat foot in adults.

FJ1461M.summary: A thin muscle on the inside of the front of the rib cage.
FJ1461M.function: Draws the costal cartilages down in expiration.

FJ1441M.summary: The deep part of the quadriceps, lying on the front of the femur under rectus femoris.

FJ1442M.summary: The largest part of the quadriceps, on the outer thigh.
FJ1442M.clinical: Preferred site for intramuscular injections in infants.

FJ1443M.summary: The part of the quadriceps on the inner thigh, bulging just above the knee.
FJ1443M.function: Extends the knee and steadies the patella in its groove.
FJ1443M.clinical: Wastes quickly after knee injury; strengthening it helps patellar tracking.

FJ2788.summary: The inner part of the thyroarytenoid lying beside the vocal ligament.
FJ2788.function: Fine-tunes the tension of the vocal fold.

FJ1448.summary: The tendinous seam running down the midline of the abdomen from the xiphoid to the pubis.
FJ1448.function: Joins the aponeuroses of the flat abdominal muscles of both sides.
FJ1448.clinical: Midline surgical incisions pass through it; it may widen after pregnancy (diastasis).

FJ1478M.summary: Long head of left biceps brachii is part of the biceps brachii. The two-headed muscle on the front of the upper arm, from the scapula to the radius.
FJ1478M.function: Flexes the elbow and, most powerfully, supinates the forearm (turning the palm up).
FJ1478M.clinical: Rupture of the long head tendon produces a 'Popeye' bulge in the arm.

FJ1395M.summary: Long head of left biceps femoris is part of the biceps femoris. The lateral hamstring, with a long head from the ischium and a short head from the femur, inserting on the fibula.
FJ1395M.function: Flexes the knee and extends the hip; the main lateral rotator of the flexed knee.
FJ1395M.clinical: Hamstring tears are the commonest sprinting injury.

FJ1479M.summary: Long head of left triceps brachii is part of the triceps brachii. The three-headed muscle on the back of the upper arm, inserting on the olecranon of the ulna.
FJ1479M.function: The main extensor of the elbow, essential for pushing and throwing.
FJ1479M.clinical: Supplied by the radial nerve; weakness of extension follows radial nerve injury.

FJ1478.summary: Long head of right biceps brachii is part of the biceps brachii. The two-headed muscle on the front of the upper arm, from the scapula to the radius.
FJ1478.function: Flexes the elbow and, most powerfully, supinates the forearm (turning the palm up).
FJ1478.clinical: Rupture of the long head tendon produces a 'Popeye' bulge in the arm.

FJ1395.summary: Long head of right biceps femoris is part of the biceps femoris. The lateral hamstring, with a long head from the ischium and a short head from the femur, inserting on the fibula.
FJ1395.function: Flexes the knee and extends the hip; the main lateral rotator of the flexed knee.
FJ1395.clinical: Hamstring tears are the commonest sprinting injury.

FJ1479.summary: Long head of right triceps brachii is part of the triceps brachii. The three-headed muscle on the back of the upper arm, inserting on the olecranon of the ulna.
FJ1479.function: The main extensor of the elbow, essential for pushing and throwing.
FJ1479.clinical: Supplied by the radial nerve; weakness of extension follows radial nerve injury.

FJ1396M.summary: Medial head of left flexor hallucis brevis is part of the flexor hallucis brevis. A short muscle in the sole with two heads inserting on the big toe.
FJ1396M.function: Flexes the big toe at its base.

FJ1397M.summary: Medial head of left gastrocnemius is part of the gastrocnemius. The two-headed calf muscle forming the bulge of the calf, from the femoral condyles to the Achilles tendon.
FJ1397M.function: Plantar flexes the ankle (rising on the toes) and helps flex the knee; the power muscle of walking, running and jumping.
FJ1397M.clinical: 'Tennis leg' is a tear of the medial head; calf strains are common in sport.

FJ1480M.summary: Medial head of left triceps brachii is part of the triceps brachii. The three-headed muscle on the back of the upper arm, inserting on the olecranon of the ulna.
FJ1480M.function: The main extensor of the elbow, essential for pushing and throwing.
FJ1480M.clinical: Supplied by the radial nerve; weakness of extension follows radial nerve injury.

FJ1396.summary: Medial head of right flexor hallucis brevis is part of the flexor hallucis brevis. A short muscle in the sole with two heads inserting on the big toe.
FJ1396.function: Flexes the big toe at its base.

FJ1397.summary: Medial head of right gastrocnemius is part of the gastrocnemius. The two-headed calf muscle forming the bulge of the calf, from the femoral condyles to the Achilles tendon.
FJ1397.function: Plantar flexes the ankle (rising on the toes) and helps flex the knee; the power muscle of walking, running and jumping.
FJ1397.clinical: 'Tennis leg' is a tear of the medial head; calf strains are common in sport.

FJ1480.summary: Medial head of right triceps brachii is part of the triceps brachii. The three-headed muscle on the back of the upper arm, inserting on the olecranon of the ulna.
FJ1480.function: The main extensor of the elbow, essential for pushing and throwing.
FJ1480.clinical: Supplied by the radial nerve; weakness of extension follows radial nerve injury.

FJ1548M.summary: Small deep muscles between the lumbar transverse processes.

FJ1548.summary: Small deep muscles between the lumbar transverse processes.

FJ1398M.summary: Oblique head of left adductor hallucis is part of the adductor hallucis. A muscle of the sole with an oblique and a transverse head inserting on the big toe.
FJ1398M.function: Adducts the big toe and supports the transverse arch.

FJ1481M.summary: Oblique head of left adductor pollicis is part of the adductor pollicis. A fan-shaped muscle in the web of the thumb with oblique and transverse heads.
FJ1481M.function: Adducts the thumb and gives the pinch its power.
FJ1481M.clinical: Weakness produces Froment's sign in ulnar nerve palsy.

FJ1398.summary: Oblique head of right adductor hallucis is part of the adductor hallucis. A muscle of the sole with an oblique and a transverse head inserting on the big toe.
FJ1398.function: Adducts the big toe and supports the transverse arch.

FJ1481.summary: Oblique head of right adductor pollicis is part of the adductor pollicis. A fan-shaped muscle in the web of the thumb with oblique and transverse heads.
FJ1481.function: Adducts the thumb and gives the pinch its power.
FJ1481.clinical: Weakness produces Froment's sign in ulnar nerve palsy.

FJ2781.summary: Oblique part of left cricothyroid is part of the cricothyroid. A muscle on the outside of the larynx between the cricoid and thyroid cartilages, the only laryngeal muscle supplied by the external laryngeal nerve.
FJ2781.function: Tilts the thyroid cartilage forward to stretch the vocal ligaments and raise the pitch of the voice.

FJ2799.summary: Oblique part of right cricothyroid is part of the cricothyroid. A muscle on the outside of the larynx between the cricoid and thyroid cartilages, the only laryngeal muscle supplied by the external laryngeal nerve.
FJ2799.function: Tilts the thyroid cartilage forward to stretch the vocal ligaments and raise the pitch of the voice.

FJ1399M.summary: A small, often incomplete muscle of the sole beside the fifth metatarsal.
FJ1399M.function: Draws the fifth metatarsal toward the sole.

FJ1482M.summary: A deep hypothenar muscle along the fifth metacarpal.
FJ1482M.function: Cups the palm by drawing the fifth metacarpal forward.

FJ1399.summary: A small, often incomplete muscle of the sole beside the fifth metatarsal.
FJ1399.function: Draws the fifth metatarsal toward the sole.

FJ1482.summary: A deep hypothenar muscle along the fifth metacarpal.
FJ1482.function: Cups the palm by drawing the fifth metacarpal forward.

FJ2749.summary: The fibrous seam down the midline of the back of the pharynx.
FJ2749.function: Joins the constrictor muscles of the two sides.

FJ1400.summary: A muscle along the inner border of the sole.
FJ1400.function: Abducts and flexes the big toe and supports the medial arch.

FJ1483.summary: The superficial muscle of the thenar eminence at the base of the thumb.
FJ1483.function: Moves the thumb away from the palm.
FJ1483.clinical: Wastes in carpal tunnel syndrome because it is supplied by the median nerve.

FJ1484.summary: A deep forearm muscle whose tendon reaches the first metacarpal.
FJ1484.function: Abducts and extends the thumb at its base.

FJ1401.summary: A short adductor muscle beneath adductor longus.
FJ1401.function: Adducts the thigh and assists hip flexion.

FJ1402.summary: The most superficial adductor, from the pubis to the middle of the femur.
FJ1402.function: Adducts the thigh, bringing the legs together.
FJ1402.clinical: The usual site of 'groin strain' in football and hockey.

FJ1403.summary: The largest adductor, a broad triangular sheet on the inner thigh with an adductor and a hamstring part.
FJ1403.function: Adducts the thigh; its hamstring part extends the hip.
FJ1403.clinical: The femoral artery passes through its adductor hiatus to reach the back of the knee.

FJ1404.summary: The upper, partly separate portion of adductor magnus.
FJ1404.function: Adducts and laterally rotates the thigh.

FJ1485.summary: A small triangular muscle at the back of the elbow.
FJ1485.function: Assists triceps in extending the elbow and stabilises the joint.

FJ2791.summary: A muscle in the aryepiglottic fold.
FJ2791.function: Helps close the inlet of the larynx during swallowing.

FJ1486.summary: A broad muscle lying under the biceps, from the humerus to the ulna.
FJ1486.function: The strongest flexor of the elbow, working in every position of the forearm.

FJ1487.summary: The muscle forming the bulk of the lateral forearm, from the humerus to the distal radius.
FJ1487.function: Flexes the elbow, most effectively with the forearm midway between pronation and supination.

FJ1405.summary: The Achilles tendon: the thickest and strongest tendon in the body, from the calf muscles to the heel.
FJ1405.function: Transmits the pull of gastrocnemius and soleus to the calcaneus to lift the heel.
FJ1405.clinical: Rupture feels like a kick to the back of the ankle; tendinopathy affects runners.

FJ1524.summary: Deep rotator muscles of the cervical spine.

FJ2547.summary: A muscle behind the levator ani from the ischial spine to the coccyx.
FJ2547.function: Supports the pelvic floor and flexes the coccyx.

FJ1342.summary: The fibrous ring at the apex of the orbit from which the four rectus muscles arise.
FJ1342.function: Anchors the rectus muscles; the optic nerve and the nerves to the eye muscles pass through it.

FJ1488.summary: A small muscle from the coracoid process to the middle of the humerus.
FJ1488.function: Flexes and adducts the arm at the shoulder.

FJ1556.summary: A muscle with two bellies joined by a tendon slung from the hyoid bone.
FJ1556.function: Opens the mouth by lowering the mandible and raises the hyoid in swallowing.

FJ1489.summary: A muscle on the back of the forearm to the third metacarpal.
FJ1489.clinical: Its origin at the lateral epicondyle is the site of tennis elbow.

FJ1490.summary: A muscle on the back of the forearm to the second metacarpal.
FJ1490.function: Extends and abducts the wrist, as in making a fist.

FJ1472.summary: A muscle along the ulnar side of the back of the forearm to the fifth metacarpal.

FJ1491.summary: A slender muscle with a tendon to the little finger.

FJ1492.summary: The main extensor of the fingers, whose tendons fan across the back of the hand.

FJ1406.summary: A muscle on the front of the leg whose tendons reach the four lesser toes.
FJ1406.function: Extends the toes and dorsiflexes the foot.

FJ1407.summary: A small muscle on the top of the foot reaching the big toe.

FJ1408.summary: A deep muscle of the front of the leg with a tendon to the big toe.
FJ1408.function: Extends the big toe and dorsiflexes the ankle.
FJ1408.clinical: Its strength tests the L5 nerve root.

FJ1493.summary: A deep forearm muscle with a tendon to the index finger.
FJ1493.function: Extends the index finger independently, as in pointing.

FJ1494.summary: A small muscle with a tendon to the base of the thumb.
FJ1494.function: Extends the thumb at its middle joint.
FJ1494.clinical: Inflamed with abductor pollicis longus in De Quervain's tenosynovitis.

FJ1495.summary: A deep forearm muscle whose tendon forms the ulnar border of the anatomical snuffbox.
FJ1495.function: Extends the thumb tip and lifts the thumb away from the palm.

FJ1452.summary: The largest and most superficial of the flat abdominal muscles, with fibres running like hands in pockets.
FJ1452.function: Compresses the abdomen, flexes and rotates the trunk, and helps forced expiration.
FJ1452.clinical: Its aponeurosis forms the inguinal ligament and the outer ring of the inguinal canal.

FJ1409.summary: A muscle of the outer leg inserting on the base of the fifth metatarsal.
FJ1409.function: Everts the foot and steadies the ankle.
FJ1409.clinical: Violent inversion can avulse the fifth metatarsal base at its attachment.

FJ1410.summary: A muscle on the outer side of the leg whose tendon crosses under the sole to the first metatarsal.
FJ1410.function: Everts and plantar flexes the foot and supports the arches.
FJ1410.clinical: Its nerve, the superficial fibular nerve, is injured by ankle sprains.

FJ1411.summary: A small muscle beside extensor digitorum longus reaching the fifth metatarsal.

FJ1412.summary: Quadratus plantae: a muscle of the sole attached to the tendon of flexor digitorum longus.
FJ1412.function: Straightens the pull of flexor digitorum longus on the toes.

FJ1496.summary: A forearm muscle from the medial epicondyle to the base of the second and third metacarpals.
FJ1496.clinical: The radial pulse is felt just lateral to its tendon.

FJ1413.summary: A muscle in the middle of the sole with tendons to the four lesser toes.
FJ1413.function: Flexes the toes at their middle joints.

FJ1414.summary: A deep calf muscle whose tendons cross the sole to the four lesser toes.
FJ1414.function: Flexes the toes and helps plantar flex the foot.

FJ1497.summary: A deep forearm muscle whose tendons pass through those of the superficialis to reach the fingertips.
